This Company is formed for the purpose of acquiring the business established by Mr. Hermann Loog. in February, 1876 (afterwards trading with six nominal Shareholders as Her- mann Loog. Limited), at 128, London Wall, London. to which premises the tveta adjoining houses, Nos. 126 Red 127, London Wall have been since added; also a second wholesale ware- house at 23 and 25. Jamaica-street. Glasgew, besides about 50 retail branches and sub-depBts, as per particulars on front sheet, and certain Patent Bights for the Double lock-Stitch Sewine Machine, the Patent N(rdie-Threader. and improve- ments in Invalids' and Children's Carrerges. The busine et is tbat of manufacturers and dealers in Sewing and other do- mestie labeur sa- log Machines, Clocks. Watches, Planes, Har- moniums, A meTican Organs, and other Musical Instrument., also Furniture, Children's and Invalids' Carriages, diR The principal lecture of the trade is to supply all Classes with do- mestic, social, and industrial labour and time-saving, as well as money-earning machinery, furniture, &L.... on the Hire- /out-chase eystem, on easy terms of payment, in point of fact, helping others to help themselves. To manufacture and buy for cash, and sell wholesale, or on easy terms of payment, a very large capital is aiways required whilst, on the other hand, the business involves such an amount of labour that no individual possessing sufficient capital for its successful working would care to undertake the labour required. Therefore it is an organisa- tion essentially adapted for Joint Stock Enterprise. The gross profits for the nine months ending September 30th. 1836, amount to £19,500, and it requires now but increased capital to double this result, with a moderate increase in toe experses, to secure a divlsable profit of £l5 per cent. on the capital now to be issued. Mr. Hermann Loog is the Patentee of a Double Lock-ertitch Sewing Machine, for which there is an absolute want, and Vir Well cannot fail to Increase the demand for his Machines, as well as considerably augment the profits. This gaebine can be seen at work at the Company's Office, when it will be ascertained that it is the only Sewing Machine in existence snaking a real Donb'e Lock-Sti`ch—that is to say, the machine makes a positive knot after every stitch, as against the twist of the two threads of the so-called Lock- Stitch Machines This knot is invaluable for most work Mr. Hermann Loog has also just taken out Patents for a Needle- means of which any person can thread a needle this will not only assist to increase his trade in Needle- Threader, read e blindfolded;r , by &awing Machines, but it will also form an item of considerable extra profit. The low price of a Shilling has been fixer.% so as to suPP'Y the milrion, whilst its cost, as per con- tracts about to be completed with a manufacturer in the North of Englaad, will not be more than a few pence each. Mr. Herm ann Loog is also the Patentee of two Important irn- provemente in another branch of his business, namely, Invalids' and Childreo's Carriages, in which department it also only requires additional capital to increase the annual sale from 6,00 to 10.00 carriages or more: The working of these patents alone will be sufficient to guarantee a substantial divi- dend on the carrital now to be issued. As for Dome,tic Ma- chinery, such as Washine Machines, Mangles, also Furniture, Harmoniums, Organs, tc , In view of the continually increas- ing demand, Mr. Her mann Loog has completed arrangements with the oldest manufacturers in Yorkshire, Scotland, and London, enabling him to sell at manufacturer's own prices. None of the goods manufactured or dealt in by the Company are liable to anY of the usual trade risks, to which almost all goods are sueject (fashion, colour, season, rfcc , ), nor does the business of the Company become in any way affected by general trade depression, nearly all the articles for sale being articles which not only earn their own costs in a short time,but prove a source of regular income in many a family. The Hire-purchase system ensures immunity against Bad Debts. The vendor will sell to the Company the assets necessary for the continuation and development of the business at their ab- solute value. Se will take no cash for his patents or goodwill, and will undertake to give his services as managing eirector for three years without any remuneration, taking for his goodwill, patents, and services Deferred Shares for £50,000, in other words, be will not get a penny until the Preferential Shareholders have received a dividend of 6 per cent per an- num, and a further bonus of 25 per cent out of the surplus profits, the remaining 75 Per cent of which will then be availa- ble for the Deferred Shares. The first quarterly dividend on the Preferential Shares will be payable December 31st, 1886. The vendor being the Promoter of the Company, there will be no promotion money Paid, and all expenses up to allotment, Including registration fees, advertising, legal charges. &c except brokerage. will be borne by him. The - present capital in the tusiness will remain in the new Company, tee Vendor taking Preferential Shares for the same. The business vrill be taken over with such of the existing con- tracts the Directors mei' approve of. These are of the ordin- ary trade character, but too numerous to specify. Subscribers will be held to have notice thereof and to have waived their right to be supplied with particulare.—Companies Act. 1867. sec. 38. Prospectuses and Forms of Application for Shares may be obtained at the Offices of the Company.

, And the children run up and and down .. The steps that lead to bird-town, . _ . - And they peep at the nests so brown . And so empty this autumn day. .-._ • - , •—•• , Soon Winter will finish his reign, . '.• - And Spring will not smile all in vain, For the nests will be patched up again, And Nature once more will be gay. , ' -'• v—Lite Folks. . 0-...., -

IN THE GARDEN. BY FRANCES L. MACE. . Was it thou.-Mignonette? For while the South Wind stills his low complaints To bear the censer of thy rich perfume, I read, upon a terrace -warm with bloom, Flower-stories of the Virgin and the Saints. I read that Mary, passing through a field, Her heart oppressed witu that mysterious gloom ' Which ever falls on those whom heaven has sealed For glory's crown—and doom. stooped often, in her meditative walk, To pluck some favoured blossom from its stalk. Some happy flower, which bowed its beauteous head And Summer's odorous benediction shed. But one poor fragile weed, ! Nor beautiful nor sweet, she would never heed But that it clung so close about her feet. With tender touch she gathered ; to her breast And to her lips the slighted floweret pressed, Because so frail, so hopeless, loved the best Ch, then the pale weed strove To whisper forth its rapture and its love: And while it mutely trembled and adored, Like praise of spirit risen From long and woful prison, A tide of fragrance from its heart was poured! N Tr once in all the ages has it sighed " For beauty's con c nal of brilliant hue, - Red of the rose, or violet's winsome blue, __. _ _
By that one kiss of pity glorified. The garden's lowly, well-beloved sower, A miraelo of sweetness from that hour— Mignonette, was it thou? —Harper's Monthly .ifayn:iue.

There has been a disposition on the part of those who have not really understood the subject to depreciate the use of standards for pure-bred poultry. They have argued that because in a few instances these standards have been carried to a ridiculous length, and that in some other cases the original merits have beer. lost sight of and the economic overborne by others that are of a merely fancy nature. The whole principle is at fault, forgetting that in no case does "one swallow make a summer." The misapplication of a principle is no proof that the principle itself is wrong. Therefore, granting that in a few instances standards have been badly framed, and that in others mere minor points have been ; developed to an injurious extent, surely that is not suffi- cient to condemn the whole of our present standards. ; We are firmly convinced that it is very largely:owing to ; these standards that we have so much of uniformity, and we are equally certain that whilst they:might be greatly improved in many ways, they have been the : means of doing great good. When it is considered that in this country we have nobody which in any way I can be regarded as a representative one, for such work ; as the settlement of such questions as this, and that in I the majority of cases what standards there are have ' been formed by private individuals or by the concur- rence of a few individuals, it is surprising that they are so satisfactory. The plan adopted in America is much better. There a body known as the American Poultry Association publishes the standard, and which only admits thereto such breeds as it deems to be fit. The plan adopted by this association of revising its standards every five years is also an admirable one, as it prevents antiquated notions being imposed upon any generation of breeders. Without such a proviso as this there would be grave danger of the standards being maintained long after they were out of date. It may not be generally known, but it is a fact, that certain external characteristics al- most always accompany certain internal characteristics. This is the law of correlative variation spoken of by Darwin. The ninth annual meeting of the Council of the National Liberal Federation was held on Wednes- day afternoon at the Albert Hall, Leeds. Sir James Kitson, Bart. (president of the Federation), was in the chair, and there were also present the Right Hon. john Morley, M.P., Lord Houghton, Lord Bur- ton, Mr. H. 11. Fowler, ALP., the Right Hon. J. G. Shaw Lefevre, M.P., Mr. Herbert J. Gladstone, M.P., Sir B. Foster (chairman of Committee of Federa- tion), and many other members of Parliament. Delegates were also present from the National Re- form Union, the London and Counties National Liberal Union, and from Liberal organisations in all parts of the United Kingdom. In the annual report, which was taken as read, the Committee gave an account of the work of the year. The report Concluded: " The Committee ap- peal with confidence to their friends in all parts of the United Kingdom for the support which is neces- sary to carry on their work. They confidently anticipate for the Federation a wider sphere of in- fluence and an ever-increasing usefulness in organ- ising the party and helping to direct its policy. The success which has attended the Federation in the past has been attained under conditions which did not admit of its fullest growth. It now seeks by the equal co-operation of every one of its federated associations to collect and express with irresistible strength the deliberate convictions of the Liberals of Great Britain. Wide enough to embrace every section of the Liberal party, honest enough to give due weight to the opinions of all, and Liberal in its widest and highest sense, the Federation looks forward to a future even more fruitful of good to the cause of Liberalism than has been its honour- able past."

That lived in Drury Lane? The Duke died in January, 1669, leaving the above- mentioned son Christopher, who became, or at all events was called, the second duke, who was appointed Gover- nor of Jamaica in 1687, and died there without issue in the same year, when his titles became extinct. A few years later, namely, in November 1700, a cause celebre was heard at the Bar of the King's Bench, in which the name of Anne Clarges, Duchess of Albemarle, was brought prominently before the public. It as an action for trespass between William Shei-win, plaintiff, and Sir Walter Clarges, Bart, defendant. The plaintiff, as heir and representative of Thomas Monk, Esq., elder brother of Qreorge, Duke of Albemarle, claimed the manor of Sutton, in Yorkshire, and also other lands in Newton, Eaton Bridge, and Shipton, as heir-at-law to the said Duke, against the defendant, to whom they had been left by his only son and successor Christopher, the second duke. At the trial several witnesses were brought for- ward to swear that they had seen Thomas Ratford, her Grace's first husband, tlive as lately as January, 1669-70, many years after her marriage with the first duke, and at the birth of the second. In opposition to this evidence it was contended that all along, during the lives of the Dukes George and Christopher, this matter was never questioned ; that the latter was universally received as the lawful son of the former, and, further, that the matter had been thrice already tried at the Bar of the King's Bench, where the defendant had gained three ver- dicts. One witness swore that he owed Ratford five or six pounds, which lie had never demanded; and a man who had married a cousin of the Duke of Albemarle swore that he had been told by his wife that Ratford died five or six years before the Duke married. The "benefit of the doubt" was given by the judge to the side of equity and leniency. In summing up, Lord Chief Justice Holt thus addressed the jury:" If you are certain that Duke Christopher was born whilst Thomas Ratford was living, you must find for the plaintiff; if you believe that he was born after Ratford was dead, or that nothing, appears of what became of him after Duke George mar- ried his wife, you must find for the defendant." In the end a verdict w:ls given for the defendant, who was the only son of Sir Thomas Clarges, brother of the Duchess, and who was created a baronet in 1674; he owned the property on which Clarges-street, Piccadilly, now stands. It only remains to add that " Nan " Clarges, Duchess of Albemarle and ex-sempstress, died within a few days of the Duke, her husband, in January, 1669, and was buried by his side in Henry the Seventh's Chapel in West- minster Abbey.

After the report for the past year had been adop- ted, together with the balance sheet—which showed an amount in hand of ..-C4s9—a resolution moved by the President, seconded by the Hon. Philip Stan- hope, and supported by Mr. John Morley was unani- mously and enthusiastically passed, expressing con- tinued and unabated confidence in Mr. Gladstone as the leader of the Liberal party. In the course of his address Mr. Morley declared that, whatever else Liberals throughout the country intended, they meant to stand firm by their old policy and by their old leader. With regard to Ireland the Liberal party stood in precisely the same position now, as in June last. The late Government never said that they wanted to carry the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill. They were willing to accept suggestions made in good faith ; but to the principle of the bill they would adhere, "with a confidence and persistency of intention which no- thing could shake." If union amongst the sections of the Liberal party could not be obtained without a surrender of principle by the enormous majority of the party to a small, though he admitted a select, minority, then there was nothing for it but to face the facts and to fight the battle out. There was no wish to proscribe individuals or to excommunicate sections of the party, but those who were parties to bringing in the Irish bills would be the most con- temptible of men if, after having lodged a protest of that magnitude and moment, they were to come before the country and ask that all might be for- given and forgotten. The upshot of that great meeting, he took it, would be the deliberate affir- mation by the great bulk of the Liberal party that the proposals of the late Government contained in them the germs of a durable settlement of the Irish question, and that upon no other lines was any settlement possible. The Conference afterwards passed a resolution declaring it to be the true policy of Great Britain to avoid all entanglement in Continental quatrels, in order that some prospect may be afforded of a reduction in the expenditure upon the army and navy.

On Monday night a lecture entitled "What is a workingman to gain by being a Conservative ?" was given in the Town Hall; Newton, by Mr. Wor- maid Waring, of the National Reform Union. Mr. Urquhart presided, and there was a fair attendance. In his introductory remarks the Chairman said he could not understand working-men being Tory. He was sure that neither a working-man nor a middle- man studied his own interest in being Tory, be- cause in Toryism there was no progress. They wanted to go forward, and indeed they must go forward, for to stand still would not do in these times. It was a pity; he thought, that the rising generation did not read the history of the past 80 years more than they did, for it gave them a lesson well worth digesting. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt about one thing, and that was that the posi- tion of the people was greatly different to what it was formerly, and they could not say that their Tory friends had brought about that difference, al- though if they were to take into account their present Chancellor of the Exchequer, he was knock- ing them all out. (Laughter.) The upper ten, how- ever, had always taken very good care to try to suit themselves in every way. But the scales must be turned now, and working-men must see that they improve the laws as they go along. (Applause.) Mr. WAILING then gave his lecture. He said that in discussing that question it would be well to de- fine the meaning of the phrases " working-man" and Conservative.'" A workingman, in the wider acceptation of the term was a man who wrote their books, who sung their songs, who edited their news- papers, and who managed their great centres of in- dustry. By training these men were working-men, but he meant particularly by that term a man who, to use the definitition given by Mr. Bright a few years ago, was one who was accustomed regularly to some useful employment or work. Then what was a Conservative? He had been a little apprehensive the week previous that th e title of his lecture would be out of place, because they would know that there was a proposal made at Bradford that the term " Conservative " should be dropped, and the word " Progressive" adopted in its place. (Laughter.) But fortunately they kept to the word Conserva- tive. A Conservative had been defined as a man who collared all he could, and kept all he got— (laughter)—and George Thompson, in the anti-corn law days, said that Conservatives meant those who, having got what did not belong to them, intended to keep it, and that those who to-day seized that which was not their own became a Conservative the day after. (Laughter.) A friend of his said there were two words that exactly conveyed the meaning of Liberalism and Conservatism, the word for Liberalism being sympathy, and for Conservatism, selfishness; and John Bright said, not a year ago, that Conservatism was selfishness, the length and the breadth and the thickness and the depth of which it was impossible to measure and to estimate. (Laughter and applause.) But lest there should be a Conservative working-man present who might feel offended with any of these definitions, he pre- ferred to take another from Chamber's dictionary, and this was the definition of Conservative there given: "One opposed to political changes; one who desired to preserve the existing institutions of his country." In his opinion Conservatism had to be coerced into action. (Hear, hear.) Had it not been so in the past? Had there been any change for the advantage of the Working-man effected by the Conservatives that had not been wrung from them by the earnest spirits in the Liberal ranks. (Hear, hear.) If they took the ques- tion of food, what had conservatism done for the working-man in the past, and what did it propoSe to do at present? EVENING- ArEETING. In the evening a great public meeting was 'held in the Colisseum, presided over by Mr. John Morley. The hall will accomodate some 4.500 people, and it was filled to its utmost capacity. An overflow gathering was held in the Town Hall, under the chairmanship of Mr. Herbert J. Gladstone. Mr. Morley was supported at the Colisseum by the members of Parliament who were present at the Conference, and by Sir William Vernon Harcourt. A magnificent reception was accorded to both Liberal leaders. _ _ _

Mr. Morley -Presided, and reviewed the proceed- ings of the afternoon. He doubted very, much the Radical proposals dangled by Lord R. Churchill be- fore the Bradford electors. Without desiring to say anything harsh of the dissident Liberals, he thought it was their duty to insist upon the Governs. ment dealing without delay with the Irish ques- tion.—Sir William • Harcourt, in addressing the meeting, ascribed the present tranquility in Ireland, not to the firm Tory administration, but to the remedial legislation persistently applied to Ireland by Mr. Gladstone, and to the reasonable expectation that with the assistance of the Liberal party the Irish people would get self-government in accordance with their wishes. He described Lord R. Churchill's dec- laration that the whole Government policy would be subordinated to maintaining the Unionist alliance as the most contemptible, humiliating, and dis- honest profession of political faith of which he had ever heard. The most startling conversion of the Tory party was on the question of Parliamentary procedure—a question on which they opposed and defeated the moderate proposals of Mr. Gladstone's Government. On the land question also they had gone over to Mr. Collings, and the celebrated doc- trine of three acres and a cow was now practically adopted as an article of the Tory creed. He was happy to see also that the Government were repen- tant 'on their foreign policy, The Treaty of Berlin had been crumbling to pieces ever since it was made, and he hoped that we had heard the last of Russophobism and Jingoism. •There was nothing in the situation now to cause despondency or disap- pointment. Out of office, the Liberals were masters of the situation; the necessities of the Tory Gov- ernment compelled them to be the instrument of the Liberal policy, and with the Liberal party lay the heritage of ths future.—Lord Houghton pro- posed a resolution declaring the confidence of the meeting in Mr. Gladstone as the leader of the Libe- ral party and cordially approving of the resolutions adopted by.the Council of the National Liberal Federation.—Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., seconded the motion, which was passed.

" Cassell's Book of Pigeons" has now reached its 17th part, and is devoted to the Pouter, chiefly those special diseases to which it is subject. There is also the admir- able outline showing the points of this beautiful variety of the domestic pigeon. We know of no better way than for the young breeder to thoroughly get into his mind this outline if he wishes to excel in his pursuit. It will implant upon his memory in a way that will never be for- gotten what it is he must ever aim at in his breeding. The plate this month is a very fine one of blue, white, and brick Jacobins.

" Lyell's Fancy Pigeons," published at the Bazaar Office, is at the 13th part, and the coloured illustrations; of which we have before spoken, maintain their charac- ter, giving this work a beauty which no other possesses. Wattled pigeons are those chiefly dealt with in the pre- sent part.

"Wallace's British Cage Birds," published at the same office, is also in its 13th part, and the lovely coloured plate of the Blue Tits is worth all the money. There is also a plate of the Ringdove, but this is not in colours, and one of the Spotted Flycatcher. The text deals with the Magpie, the Jay, the Cuckoo, the Wryneck, the Nut- hatch, and the Green Woodpecker.

I At this season of the year it is necessary to look ahead a little, and those succeed best who do this. They are prepared for eventualities, and can meet the necessities of each season as they arise. If sand is used in the poultry houses a stock of it should now be laid in, as it is difficult to get any in wet or snowy weather; or if earth or fine ashes be used instead, let these be stored up. Old mortar, lime, or oyster shells had better be obtained also, for it is well known that the thing wanted is. not always easiest to get just when it is required. Old mor- tar is always worth securing. Either this or a supply of 1 fine gravel is necessary for shell forming and as an aid to digestion.

div.head: NAN CLARGES, DUCHESS OF ALBEMARLE.
div.p: NAN CLARGES, DUCHESS OF ALBEMARLE.

Our readers may be interested by the following sketch of Nan Clarges, wife of General Monk, who, being general in command of the forces of the Commonwealth after Cromvrell's death, went over to the side of Charles ithe Second, restored him to the throne, and amongst other rewards from the King, had the grant of the Honor of Clitheroe, the superior territorial lordship in Blackburn Hundred. The sketch is extracted from the Gendloman's Magazin,. In the reign of the "Merry Monarch," courtiers and nobles, to say nothing of princes, did not always look to the highest rank in the selection of their wives • and in- deed the same to a certain extent may be said to have been the case during the puritanical times of the Com- monwealth; for within three years after the execution of Charles the First at Whitehall, the daughter of a black- smith and farrier in the Savoy,JohnClarges by name, was fortunate enough in her matrimonial career to secure for her husband no less a celebrated person than General Monk, the Duke of Albemarle. To John Clarges is attri- buted the setting up of the Maypole in the Strand at the time of the Restoration, upon the site. Clarges was farrier to the Duke. then plain Colonel Monk. He lived over his forge at the junction of tho Strand and Drury- lane, near the spot where the historic " Maypole " was set up. He gave his daughter an education suited to the employment to which she was brought up, namely, that of a milliner. As the manners of young people are gene- rally formed in early life, Anne—or as she was usually called "Nan "—Clarges retained something of the black- smith's daughter about her even after her elevation to a a coronet with strawberry leaves. On one fine morning in the summer of 1632 Anne Clarges was married, in the church of St. Lawrence Poulteny, in the City of London, to one Thomas Ratford, the son of another man of the same name, who had been a farrier, and a servant in the employment of Prince Charles, and was resident in the "Mews," no doubt the King's Mews at Charing Cross, on the spot now covered by the National Gallery. After the marriage we are told that this Thomas Ratford and his wife lived at the "New Exchange," in the Strand, in a house or shop bearing the sign of the "Three Spanish Gipsies." Here they sold such articles of domestic use and requisites for the toilet as wash-balls, powders, and gloves ; Mistress Anne Rat- ford also teaching plain and fancy needlework to such young girls as, wishing to acquire the art and mystery of a semptress, chose to avail themselves of her services. About 1647 Mistress Ratford 'was herself acting as semp- tress to Colonel Monk; she used to carry his linen to his military quarters, and, as it is alleged, "had great control and authority over him." It is even said that when Monk was in " durance vile," in the Tower of London, she was kind to him in more than one capacity. It must be remembered that he was then in want, and that she assisted him ; and when afterwards she became his wife he had so high an opinion of her understanding that he often consulted her in important matters. As she was a thorough Royalist, it is probable that she really had a hand in bringing about the restoration of the monarchy. But nothing is more certain than that the brave corn- mender, who was never afraid of bullets, was often terri- fied by the tongue of his wife. In 1648 her father and mother died, and in the fol- lowing year, some little domestic squabble or grievance having arisen, she and her husband separated. Whether Anne Clarges (or Ratford) had given up her stall in the New Exchange, or whether her linsband was really dead, is not, and never will be known, for no certificate from any parish register appears to have been forthcoming to prove his burial: but at all events, in 1652, the lady her- self saw no impediment to her entering a second time into the connubial state, and accordingly in the above- mentioned year she: was married at the church of St. George the Martyr, in Southwark, to the gallant colonel, a name of importance in English history, and one whom we afterwards know as the chief instrument of the re- storation of monarchy. In the following year she was delivered of a son, Christopher, of whom we shall hear more presently. In 1660 the Dukedom of Albemarle was conferred on Monk (who had now become a General), but the coronet of strawberry leaves does not appear to have rested very becomingly upon the brow of the Duchess; for as Pepys tells us in his gossiping diary, "she became the laughing- stock of the Court, and gave general disgust"—of course, he means among the ladies. Pepys tells us, by the way, how he went to Westminster Hall, and bought among other books one of the Life of our Queen, which lie read at home to his wife. " But, " he adds, "it was so sillily written that we did nothing but laugh at it.

THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION AWARDS.

On Monday the following letter appeared. in a Liverpool paper—" Mr. Clarke Aspinall, in his let- ter on Exhibition awards, asserts that the jurors were elected solely by the exhibitors themselves. We can only state that we fear he is under a delu- sion. If not, how arises the circumstance of not one gentleman named by the leather exhibitors appearing on the jury ap- pointed by the executive to include leather in its list of articles for adjudication? It is now decid- edly within our knowledge that another exhibitor of leather happened, without either of us being cognisant of the act of the other, to nominate the same two gentlemen that we ourselves did. These were gentlemen who were brought up to and who have spent the whole of their lives in the leather trade, and gentlemen in whose integrity and sound judgement not even the most sceptical would cavil at. But they were not invited. We refrain from saying more on this head, though we could if it were material. Now, as regards a more personal matter—the reference to that firm exhibiting leather. That refers to us, and arises from an error in the information supplied to us by our agent. We wrote him for a list of the articles which, in addi- tion to leather, that special jury had to decide upon and he gave us the items as named in our first let- ter to the Press, but on Thursday night last he wrote again, saying that he had made a mistake, and that the jury which had to include leather were appointed to award upon, not jams, inks, soaps, &c., as erroneously mentioned, but cookery, saucepans, pottery, artificial teeth, lamps, gums, horsenails, photograpt s, knitting-machines, green- houses, mechanical appliances, electrical and engine works, payer, safes, fire-engines, kc., but we fail to see how, in any way, the absurdity of the farce is mitigated. The one jury was not an iota less capable of discriminating the qualities of leather than the other. As for the assertion that the chairman of the jury that actually did adjudicate on leather being "probably one of the largest leather factors in the North of England," all that we can say is, that that information comes to us as a great surprise, although we have known him for twenty years, and feel quite sure that he personally would not lay claim to any such distinction. The facts are that he has boon a large hyde and tanning ma- terial factor, with a leather business gradually attaching, but as he was never known to take any active part in the management of the leather de- partment, we cannot quite understand his qualifi- cations for the post he seems to have had no hesi- tation in accepting. This is scarcely all, for why should exhibits of an important industry like leather be submitted to the judgment—were it ever so great—of a single juror? Finally, we reiterate our statements, that not only no man appointed on the jury which decided on leather was nominated by any exhibitor of that product, but also that no member of it had the slightest qualification for the duty. Yours, &C., HENRY PARKINSON and Co., Warrington, October 30, 1886.

FASTING COMPIITITION.—Signor Succi, the Milanese fast- ing man, has accepted a cli.allenge from Alexander Jacques, of Crayford, Kent, for a prolotri:ed fast as a test of endur- ance. Sued, who is to commence hi 'z fast of 50 days in about a fortnight, has arrived in Paris, accomnanied by one of his frienoq, a doctor of Milan.

CABINHI JUNCIL.—The first Cabinet Connell sinc& tire prorogation of Parliament was held at the Foreig,,_ Office on "Monday afternoon. Lord Salisbury, who had been detained at his official reaidence with Count lia,zfe,hit, arrived at the Foreign Office at a quarter to three, when the only ministers_ absent were Lords Cross aud Ashbourne.

ST. HELENS ASSOCIATION V HAYDOCK RECREATION. The first teams of these clubs met on the ground of the latter, at Havdock. on Saturday afternoon. The game was very exciting, but the visitors had the best of the play throughout, and won by six goals to three. LANCASHIRE JUNIOR CHALLENGE CUp.—EARLESTOWN V. WHEELTON.—A few weeks ago the Esrlestown Club met Wheelton ie the first round of the competition fer the Lan- cashire Junior Challenge Cup and defeated them by eleven goals to one. Owing to the victors having played a "pro- fessional," the Committee of the Lancashire Association ordered the tie to be replayed at Wheelton, and in accord- ance with this decision the teams again met at Wheelton on Saturday. The Earlestonians had the best of the game throughout, and again asserted their superiority by scoring four goals to none.

I was stated in evidenc3 Oat tl)e respondent eloped to Ireland with a fiewer girl known ns Rocky, upon whom be had tpEnt £l,OOO. WIFE MURDER BY A DRUNKARD. At the Newcastle AFSiZeS, on Saturday, Patrick Judge, 48, a fish hawker, was suatencad to death for the murder of his wife by shoot- ing her. The woman had left the prisoner, who seems to have been actuated by jealousy, and to have made the fatal attack upon her while he was suffering from delirium tremens.

SEVERE STOBIL—A severe storm %f wind and rain pre• veiled almost all over the United Kingdom on Tuesday night and on Wednesday morning. The gale appears ta have rsz,ed with great force in Scotlani, from where seve- ral accidents, fatal and otherwise, besides much destruction of property, are reported. A Fowey schooner was wrecked on Wednesday night on Thorpnns, on the Fuffolk coast. Two lifeboats proceeded in a heavy sea to the spot, and saved the crew of swen men.

NOTES BY THE WAY. There could scarcely have been a better exposition of Rugby football than the match between Warrington and Mossley first teams on Saturday. Although Warrington had the best of the score at the finish and Vett best of the game throughout, yet on the whole the teams were so equally matched that the slightest mistake on the part of any player would have had a bad effect for his side, aad the result is mainly due to the fact that none of the Warrington players made a mistake. One point was noticed by everyone, and that is that Barnes was the best watched man on the field, and it is a very nice compliment in its way to the reputation that player has won. As usual Speaktnau and Gilbert behind the pack were on the alert to give the Warrington drop- goal kicker a chance, but it was no use for the Mossley men were d )wn the centre three-quarter in less than no time, so to speak. The game in fact was essentially a forwards game, and had it not been that an occasion d long kick of the Mossley backs gave Walsh, the Warrington full back, an opportu- nity for some smart play now and then, the work of the , backs was comparatively trifling. The play of the War- rington forwards wig of the highest class in every re- spect and to it the very honourable result of this match is chieily due. Someone signing himself "A member of the Warrington , club," writes, with respect te the match between Frodsham I and Sankey to which attention was called list week, to say that he was a spectator at the match, and that the remarks made are untrue. On arriving on the field, he says, they found that the Frodsham Rovers bad not provided a referee, and did not seem to understand the duties of a referee. He alleges that the Frodsham men created a disturbance, after giving unfair decisions, and that the Sankey men, on offer- ing to re-commence play, were told they might as well leave the field, as they should not play any more. The corres- pondence on the subject must now close so far as our columns are concerned.

THE COTTON TRADE STRIRES --The Spisners' Association of Lancaihire and adjoining counties has resolved to sup- port, at all costs, the spinners brought out on Thursday at six spmninu mills of Damen to resist the reduction of which a notice was given. Several other disputes are at hand in East Lancashire. A strike is threatened at Clay- ton-le-Moors, and ens has tilv,n place at Preston on sateens. The joint committee for North and North-east Lancashire has had another meeting on the question of a universal list.

THE LONDON SOCIALISTS' PROCSSION.—I2 view of the determination of the Sochlists in London to have a proces- sion et the unemployed fellowing the Lord Mayor's show, the police authorities are sending to the various shopkeepers along the line of route, advising thorn to entitely close their shops during the passage of the procession, and where the windows are protected only )y iron railing, they suggest that they should be boarded up. Colonel Fraser on Tuesday night issued the regulations for traffic on Lord Mayor's Day in London, and announced that no tither procession or or- ganised body of persons will be permitted. THE ARMSTRONG Casii.—ln the Queen's Bench Division on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Maniety, John Broughton, ensband of Mrs Brougl;tn, who will be remembered for her connection with the Armstrong case, brought an action against Mr. Squire, printer and publisher, Ittel Lion-court, London, to recover damages for a libel contained in a re- publication of the " Maiden Tribute " from the "Pall Mall G•zette." The defence was a total denial of the re-pablica- tion.—The jury were unable to agree, and, after being locked no for two hours and a half, were discharged. It transpired during the hearing of the ease that the plain- tiff's 4ction against the " Pall Mall Gazette" had been settled by the payment of £2OO. TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN LONDON.—A shocking tragedy occurred early on Thursday morning in the vicinity of Russell.aquare, Bloomsbury, London. The house, 13. Montague-place, is in the occupation of Mr. Eggin and big wife, who keep a boarding establishment, th conducting of which formed their occupation. The coGIE of the house went into the kitchen at ten o'clock on Thursday morning, and was horrified to find the bodies of her master and mis- tress on the floor in pools of blood. She gave an alarm, and the police were communicated with and two doctors sum- moned, when it was found that Mr. Eggin was dead, with a bullet wound in his forehead. while Mrs. Eggin was also wounded in the heed, but was still alive. Mrs Egan was still living on Thurslay night. It appears that the mur- derer had recently been in a lunatic asylum.

We understand that the names of four members of the Warrington first team have been sent up to the County Committee, namely, Fair. Turner, Ashton (captain), Barnes, and Gilbert. It is whispered that Turner is sure ef a place in the county team.

Tho Manchester" -Examiner " has come to the conclusion that Warrington,having beaten Mosslev, may now be ranked amongst first-class clubs. The inquiry is very naturally put, " Where have they been all along ?"

ROBBERY OF DIAMONDS AND ATTEMPTED 'AI RDE R. At the Old Bailey, Monday, before Mr. Justice Smith, James Palmer was indicted for feloniously wouhding Julius Tabak, with intent to murder and Sunuel Gamb-

land, Leon Weiner, Adolphe Weiner, and David Jacoby were charged with aiding and counselling Palmer to commit the offence. The prosecutor, who is a German, carries on business in the Eus•on-road, London, as a diamond merchant, and on March 25th he was robbed of diamonds to the value of £1,400, anti at the same time

was brutally maltreated, it is alleged, by the prisoner Palmer. 'the trial of the rive men charged with complicity in the great diamond robbery was resumed at the Ofel Bailey on Thursday. when counsel :or the various prisoners addressed the jury. On Thursday the prisoners were cenvicted, and sentences passed of ten years' peeal servitude upon James Palmer. seven years upon Leon Weiner and David Jacoby, and five years upon Adolphe Weiner and Samuel Scambland. SHOCKING DOUBLE MURDER AT LYTHAINI.—A most atro- cious double murder was committed on Tuesday afternoon at Lytham, the murderer being a roan 67 years of age, named James Mellor, recently employed by the Local Board as a blacksmith, and his victims his wife and wife's sister. The former was 58 and the latter about 56 years of age. Shortly before five o'clock Mellor accosted a police consta- ble on duty. asking him to go and look at two women who had hurt themseivea. Upon reaching Mallor's house, the constable discovered Mrs. Mellor on a couch in the kitchen quite dead, with her bead shockinzly battered. In the back garden he found her sister, Miss Kent, ;Os') quite dead, and the skull smashed. The officer at once arrested Mellor, and when charged with the murder the prisoner said, "I hope You will forgive me for what I've done." Upon a search being made, a large hammer was found in the garden, besmeared with blood. The heads of the vic- tims had been beaten to pulp, sleazing the determination with which the foul deed was perpetrated. The murderer's wife appears to have been asleep when attacked. Miss Kent, who at the time of the attack, was hanging out clothes, appears to have been struck from behind. Medical men pronounced the murderer quite sane. Mellor and his wife had net lived on comfortable terms for some time past —On Wednesday, an inquest was held on the bodies of Mrs. Mellor and Miss Kent,. The circumstances disclosed showed that the crime had probahly been to a large extent premeditated. Mellor passed a restless night in the police cells, guarded by constables. His manner is described as reserved, and he makes no reference. to the crime. A ver- dict of wilful murder was returned. On Thursday Mellor was brought befere the magistrates and committed for trial. He put a number of questions to one of he sons with a view to showing that he had been ill-used by certain members of his family. . 11: U_ ON CONSUMPTIoN. 4:.--'' ONGRet'E 7.. PHYSICIAN.

To the Editor of the " Femily Doctor." Sntf----The investigations I have made on the sub- ject of kidney, liver, and Bright's Disease, conclu- sively demonstrate the fact, and I state it deliberately as a physician, that more than one-half the deaths which occur in England are caused by impaired action of the kidneys, and the consequent retention in the blood of the poisonous uric acid. In my hospital practice in England, India, South America, and also while a surgeon in the Royal Navy, I gave a great o'eal of attention to the study of dis- eases of the kidneys and urinary organs, and found that not only was the cure of chronic Bright's Disease hopeless, but that kidney disease was remarkably pre- valent—much more so than generally known—and was the cans,' of the majority of cases of sickness ; further, that the medical profession have no remedy which exerts any positive control over these organs. I had heard of Waruer's Safe Cure and its marvel- lous results, but had never felt myself at liberty to prescribe to it, as such a course would have been re- garded as irregular. But some time ago, when I had a case which resisted all regular treatment, complica- ted with the passing of renal calculi, much against ray inclination, I allowed the patient to obtain War- ner's Safe Cure and use it. It is only just to say that in this case the result was simply marvellous, as the attack was a severe one, and the prognosis very grave, for his urine contained albumen and granular tube- oasts.

The action of the medicine was singular and un- accountable to me, I had never seen anythtng like it. The patient recovered promptly, and is to-day a well and healthy man. This stimulated my inquiries into the merits of the remedy. I had an analysis made, and found it to be of a purely vegetable char- acter—'a simple tropical leaf that was not named in oar Pharmacopmia, and, indeed, was unknown to me; but I found would be harmless to take at all times and under all circumstances. Casting ',aside all professional prejudice, I determined to give the Warner's Safe Cure a thoroughly fair trial, and felt at liberty to do this, as I was anxious that my patients should be restored to health., no matter by what means. I prescribed it in a variety of cases of acute and chronic Bright's Disease, congestion of the kidneys, catarrh of the bladder ;And in every instance did i 6 speedily effect a cure. For this reason I deem it my duty to give to the world this statement regarding the value of Warner's Safe Cure. I am aware that, coming from me, known as I am throughout this country as a physician and lecturer, it will arouse considerable surprise, and possibly the animosity of my brother physicians. But I make this statement, let ms assure you, upon facts which I am prepared to produce, and which I can substantiate to the letter. I appeal to those physicians of large prac- tice, who know how fatal and common disease of the kidneys is, to lay aside their professional prejudice, give their patients Warner's Safe Cure, restore them to perfect health, earn their gratitude, and thus be true physicians in every sense of the word. Having had over seventeen years' experience in my profession, I can conscientiously and emphatically state that I have been able to give more relief and effect more cures by the use of Warner's Safe Cure than all the other medicines in the British Pharma• Copcela, the majority of which, I am sorry to say. are very uncertain in their action. W. ED. RoBSON. L.R.C.5.1., M.K.Q.C.P.1., Late R.N. New Eqham, Englefield Green, Staines, OStober 12th, 1886.

THE BULGARIAN CRISIS KAULBAR'S HARASSING TACTICS—MEETING OF THE SOBRANJE. Trutectere, SATURDAY.—G-eneral Raul bars despatched an ul- timatum to the Bulgarian Government this afternoon com- plaining of the treatment of Russian subjects in Bulgaria, and of the general system of terrorism employed by the Government, and threatening that it in three days time he does not receive a satisfactory answer he will leave Sofia with the whole Consul personell, and will throw all the res- ponsibility upon the Government. The Government has forwarded a circular to all the Prefects instructing them to take the most stringent measures to prevent any Russian subject being molested. A copy of this circular has been sent to General lieulbers, together with a request that he will indicate what Russian subjects had been molested. IRNOVA, SUNDAY.—The Sobranje was opened at eleven o'clock this morning. Punctually at the hour appointed Stambuloff and Colonel Mutenroff entered the densely crowded house, followed by the Ministers and the officers of the garrison. M. Stambuloff then read the opening speech, stating that since the abdication of the Prince the Govern- ment bad striven with success to maintain order, seouritY9 and peace in the country, and they therefore considered it their duty ta convoke the citizens in order to elect deputies for the choice of a new Prince, who would defend the liberty of the nation and lead it in the path of progress. The cou- duding words of the speech, "Long live free and indepee- dent Bulgaria," were received with loud cheers. After the reading of the speech—which was signed by all three Re- gents—was over, M. Stambaloff and Colonel Mutkuroff . withdrew, followed by the officers of the garrison. The names of the members were then called over. When the name of Mr Grantchaloff and of other deputies assassinated at Dubritze were read the Ministry and the whole house cried with one voice, " May their souls rest in peace." VIENNA, MONDAY.—On Saturday intelligence was re- ceived by the Porte from St, Petersburg that the order for the despatch of the vessels of war to Varna came direct from the Czar after frequent and long interviews with Count Schouvaloff on'the lattet's return From Berlin. Informa- Con from the same eource states that all has been prepared for the eccnpation of Bulgaria, and only the final order from the Can. is now awaited. PARIS, MONDAY —The latest information received here does not foreshadosr an early Russian occupation, and it is stated on good authority that Germany has made, and is making the greatest efforts to prevent Russia from taking a step involving, in the belief of competent judges, great probability of general trouble in Europe next spring. VIENNA, MONDAY NIGIIT.—A Russian agent provocateur has been arrested in Varna, upon whom many proclamations were found. It is BMW that M. Grecoff has declared at Constantinople that the Bulgarian Government is willing to • resign and make way for a Coalition Government in which the Zankoff party would he represented. VIENNA, Moemer.—Telegraphic advices from Tirnova announce that M. Zikoff has been elected president of the Sobranje. Gen. Kaulbars has threatened to bombard Varna if the Balgarians prevent the Russians disembarking. CONSTANTINOPLE, TUESDAY.— &nernqint; to the repeated representations of M. Gtecoff, the Bulgarian delegate, the Porte is endeavouring to h-i' about an improvement in the relations between Bulgaria and Russia through the intermediary of the Ottoman Embassy at St. Petersburg. PARIS, Turatertev.—The " Moniteur " to-day, after stating that the candidature of Prince Waldemar for the Bulgarian throne could receive the suffrages of the Great Powers, asks if the Prince would be willing to exchange a free and independent life for an existence full of anxieties and uncertainty. TIRNOVA, THUPSDAY.—A state of siege has been pro- claimed at Philippopolis, at the pressing request of the civil and military authorities, who urged the adoption of this measure owing to the bands of brigands infesting the Karlovo district. Russian agents are accused hero of being concerned in the organisatien of these hands. WARSHIPS SENT TO VARNA. PARIS, TIIESDAY.—A telegram from Vienna states that 12 Rassian war vessels have left Sebastopol for Varna, OFFICIAL PLACARDS TORN DOWN. Venere, TUESDAY.—The kavass of the Russian Consulate here, together with some Russiae sailors, have deliberately and ostentatiously torn dewn a number of official placards, containing M.' Stembonloff's recent speech. The Bulgarian authorities were aftaid to interfere, as the Russian consul threatened. if they did so, to land troops from the war vessels now in the harbour. Great exeitement prevails. AUSTRIA -HUNGARY. • Great dissatisfaction has been created at Pesth by the production of the Hungarian budget. The finances of the kingdom are in a deplorable condition, and it is believed that the Ministry will be forced to contract a loan of 36 millions of florins, and that the deficit next year will amount to 60 millions. FRANCE.—TEIE SITUATION IN ANNAM : DES- ER A.TE FIGHTING. MONDAY.—The mail from the East brines details respecting the destruction of a detachment of Tonquinese riflemen near Phun-Ho, in the province of Nam-dinh. The party, which numbered 30 men, fell into an ambuscade, and, in endeavouring to cross a river, were shot down almost to a man by some hundreds of Chines., most of whom were armed with repeating rifles. Lieut. Fongeres, who was in command of the Toncoinese, was killed about the same time. The French post of Ding Trien, near Deng Song, was attacked by twelve hundred Chinese corning from the north. The Chinese were repulsed after desperate fighting, in which they lost forty-five men. On the French side only one man was wounded. div.head: PR ESCOL
div.p: PR ESCOL
CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HoPE.--On Tuesday the usual fortnightly meeting was heid in the schoolroom. There was a good attendance of children. Mr. Thomis Haigh was chairman.

CHURCH OF ENGLAND TIDSPERANCE SOCIETY.—An en- tainment under the auspices of the Present Church of Eng- land Temperance Society was held en Monday evening, when the attendance was very good, being the *best of the present season. The chair was occupied by the R±v. H. A. Macnaghten. During the evening Mr. James Case gave an appropriate address in the absence through illness of Mr. Duncan. of St. Helens An excellent programme, provided by Mr. Stookley, was gone through, Miss Myers being the accompanist. Those who took part in the entertainment were Miss Kitty and Master Bob Duncan, Mr. Henry Ellard, Misses Myers and Mary Prescott, Master Paul Renshall, Masters Sam, 'red, and Charley Duncan. Miss Seddon ac- companied the songs of Miss Myers. PRESOOT BIORWAY BOARD.—The monthly meeting of the members was held on Tuesday. Present—Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman), Tyrer, Lowe, Cross (clerk), Golds- worth (surveyor), and W. Goldsworth (assistant surveyor). —Expenditure: Mr. Goldsworth submitted his statement of expenditure for the four weeks from September 30. h to October 28th, as follows :—Bold, £lO 63 21 ; Knowsley, £l3 5s 91 ; Rainh ill, £lO 103 6d ; Whiston. £l6 7s 8d ; team labour, £l5 133 81; new materials, £l3 0411; hie dentals, £4 18s sd; total, £B4 2s 31.—The calls: The following calls were made forthe ensuing half year :—Bold, £275 ; Knowsley, £3OO ; Rainhill, £200; Whiston, £325; total, £l,loo.—Telephones at Rain/sill : In reply to the chairman, Mr. Goldsworth said that the Telephone Com- pany had decided for the present not to proceed with the erection of the telephone poles at Rainhill.—There was no further business.

PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of the Local Board was held on Wadnesday. when there were present Messrs. James Berry, (in the chair), T. S. Preston, J. K. Slack, I'. Dannett, Goldsworth (surveyor), U. Cross (clerk), Dickinson (nuis- ance inspector), and Bixter (rate collector). FitartcE.—Mr. Bixter reported that he had collected since the last meeting £33 9s 11d, and deposited it with the treasurer. The amount in the bank was £64 13e 6j.—The chairman (to Mr. Bixter) : The whole of the rates are col- lected in ?—Mr. Bixter : Yes, sir.—The Chairman : And we have a clean book ?—Mr. Bixter : Yes sir.—The Chair- man Of course, except the irrecovearble ?—Mr. Bixter : Yes. Tog GAS.—A discussion took place in reference to the the gas supplied by the Prescot Gas Company, satn"dngt f lrti.li'reston moved, and Mr. Dennett seconded a mo- tion that the clerk write to Mr. Beckley, analyst, of Wigan, to ascertain upoa what terms he would analyse the gas sup- plied to the Prescot consumers. NEW BATE.—On the motion of Mr. Preston, seconded by Mr. Dennett, the seal of the Board was affixed to the new rate of Is 4d in the pound. BIRTHS AND DEATHS.—Mr. Fogg reported that the num- ber of deatMs for the month of October within the Board's district was 7, compued with 5 in the same month last year. The death-rate per 1,000 of the population (6,418) wis 13.08, as compared with 934 in October, 1885. The births were 22. against 21 in the same month last year. THE NEW BYE•LAWS.—The Chairman said that the sub- committee appointed to revise the bye-laws had sat three nights and had gone through almost every law with great patienee.—Mr. Slack moved that the bye-laws be approved. —Mr. Dennett seconded the motion, which was carried. THE PEOPJSED NEW WATER Blue—The Clerk said he had a letter from Mr. George J. Atkinson, the Town Clerk of Liverpool, stating that Liverpool Corporation had decided to promote a bill in Parliament to Equalise the water charges throughout the whole district of their water supply, and to remove all disadvantages which the out districts are at present under as compared with the city."—Mr. Preston seid it appeared to him from the report of the Liverpool Corporation meeting that the effect of the bill would be to raise the price of water from 9d to is in Prescet.—The Clerk said it would be increased.—The Chairman suggested that a special meeting should be held to see what the real effect of the bill would be upon the Prescot ratepayers.--Mr. Preston moved that a committee consisting of the whole Board, should meet between now and the next meeting, to consider the matter.—Mr. Dennett seconded the motion, which was carried. THE VAEANCY ON THE BOARD.—The Clerk said it was necessary to ell up the vacancy which had been caused by the death of Mr. gatton.—Mr. Preston was of opinion that the ratepayers should decide tile matter.—Mr. Slack and Mr. Dennett were of the same opinion. A NUISANCE.—The Nuisance Inspector called attention to a nuisance in Kemble-street, through the drains being stopped up.—The Surveyor was instructed to inspect the nlace, and a committee WaS appointed to consider the sanitary condition of some of the adjoining property.—This was the only business.
CHEAPEST Houss in the ciTy for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy Goods.-175. Oxford-street. Manchester.— Advt.

div.head: TRADE ORGANISATION. AT ST.
div.p: TRADE ORGANISATION. AT ST.
HELENS.

A meeting of working-men connected with the various trades of St. Helens was held in the Volunteer Hall, on Fri- day evening, for the purpose of furthering the interests and strengthening the local Trades Council. Mr. Henry Seton- Karr, M.P., presided ; and there were upon the platform Messrs. George Kelly, of the Manchester and Salford Trades Council ; T. R. Threlfall, of the Southport Trades Council ; Thomas Glover, miners' agent, St. Helena; C. Cannon and Robert Hunter, Bottlemekers' Association ; W. Battersby and W. Wogan, Miners' Society ; Councillor John Forster, Mr. H. Martin, and Mr. J. Cross. The Chairman, who was received with loud applause, said they were met together on a question which he believed to be a most important one for the inhabitants of St. Helens, and for the trade and manufactures of the district. Be read lettees of apology from Mr. James Mawdesley, of the Cotton Spinners' Amalgamated Association, Manchester, who had been announced to speak ; from Mr. Burt, M.P., Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. Birtwistle, Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., and Mr. Alfred Bailey, jun., Preston, and proceeded to say they were met together to consider the question of strengthening the Trades Union Council in St. Helens. It WAS not a party meeting. Some of them might not agree in their views of politics, or of the present political leaders, but he trusted they were all agreed, at all events, in the principle of endeavouring to do what they could to further the interests of trade and commerce, and bring about a closer union between cipital and labour. (Applause.) As he (the chairman) understood trades unions, they proposed to consult the interests, in the first place, of tbe working; classes, for they were simply an orgainsation to fully repre- sent and enable men employed to organise and act in con- cert when occasion arose. He took it that trades unions ought to do more than that. They ought to be able to fur- ' ther the interests of both employers and employed, for their interests were identical. He did not think that any action which tended to set employers against employed was wise. It could not be wise or judicious for any to advocate mea- sures which tended in that direction. (Applause.) There was a time, he believed, when trades unions used to result in strikes. Without going into details, they might be sure that if tiades unions and trades union councils resulted in setting employed against employer, and in bringing about strikes, those unions would fall in disfavour and meet with hostility from the general public of this country. (Hear, hear.) But, on the other hand, if their action resulted in preventing strikes and resulted in bringing employers and employed into closer relations and further their interests, he (the chairman) thought they ought to be supported by every thinking man and every thinking politician of the country. (Applause.) He hoped those present would listen attentively and consider well the arguments brought for- ward, and he trusted the conclusions come to would be highly beneficial to trade and commerce in the district. They had passed through, and were passing through a time of depression. There was a time when trade and commerce were flourishing, and it did not then matter much what happened. Men got good wages, and the employers made lots of money, but that was not so at the present time. He (the chairman) thought any question which affected trade and commerce was now of the utmost importance. (Applause.) Mr. George D. Kelly proposed the following resolution t— " That in the opinion of this meeting it is of the greatest importance that there should be a strong trades union coun- cil in St. Helens, and we hereby pledge ourselves to do all in our power to increase the present trades council in St. Helens."—The Chairman said he did not pledge himself in being present te agree with or be responsible for all the opinions that might be expressed on that platform, bat he had listened to Mr. Kelly with great interest, and believed if the question of technical education was advanced by trades councils, they could not possibly do any better work. (Ap• Platise.)—Mr. Threlfall seconded, and Mr. W. Wogan and Mr. Thomas Glover supported the resolution, which was carried.

div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Bishop of London has appointed Dr. Liddon to the office of chancellor in St. Paul's Cathedral, void by the death some months ago of Bishop Anderson ; and the Canon Scott-Holland to the post of precentor, in succession to the late Rev. C. A. Belli.

ANOTHER GUN FATALITY. - On Wednesday, while Mr. Joseph Bobbia, retired decorator, of Highpury, London, was cleaning a double-barrelled gun, which he did not know was loaded, the weapon exploded and shattered his wife's skull, killing her on the spot. The husband has been taken into custody.

THE TITHE AGITATION.—At a meeting of farmers in the neighborhood of Llanrwst on Tuesday evening, it was de- cided to ask Canon Jones for 25 per cent reduction in tithe, to protest against any interference of landlords with tithes, and to offer the utmost resistance to tithe being made pay- able by landlords.

The labourer George Smith, who confessed at West Ham that he murdered a girl named Pacey at Boston, Lincoln- shire, by striking her on the head and pushing her into 53Me water in September last, was on Wednesday discharged from the custody of the West Ham police and handed over to officers from Lincolnshire.

TRAGIC SUICIDE.—. 4. young man named JAmes Neill, a van driver at Greenock, after parting on Sunday with his sweetheart, a domestic servant at the west end of Greenock, walked a few yard along the road, and then deliberately fired two shots with a revolver at his breast. He expired in a few minutes. A quarrel with his relatives is assigned as the cause of the act.

At the quarterly meeting of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce. on Monday' a resolution was moved—" That, having waited in vain for more than forty years for other nations to follow England's Free Trade example. this Cham- ber thinks the time has now arrived to reconsider its posi- tion." The resolution was only defeated by one vote; 21 voted for it, and 22 against it. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WlGAN.—Joseph Ed- mondson, a platelayer, of Whittle, died OR Sunday at Wigan Infirmary from injuries received on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. On Saturday night, late, he walked up the line to Orrell, where be had to work, and, in stepping out of the way of one train, was knocked down by another. He was not found until four o'clock on Sunday morning, ' lying on the line with both legs cut off. He was removed to the infirmary, but died as stated.

FORGERY BY AN OFFICER'S VALET.—At the Manchester Assize, on Saturday, a man named Berry, who acted as vulet to Captain Molyneux, of the Duke of Lancaster's Yeomanry, pleaded guilty to a charge of forgery. The prisoner had taken the opportunity of stealing some blank cheques, which he filled up and attempted to utter. He had been previously convicted of various offences, and had served a term of penal servitude. The learned judge (Mr. Justice Cave) s-ultenced him to penal servitude for a period of ten years. _

THE- PEACE SocrerY The International Arbitration and Peace Association, having sent to the Foreign Secre- arY a copy of reselutions urging the Powers of Europe to come to an agreement so that a Prince of Bulgaria may be selected at the earliest possible date, as desired by till people of Bulgaria and for the peace of Europe, has reeeived the following reply, dated the I:3rd ult. :—" Sir,—l am di- rected by the Earl of iddesleigh to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 19th mat, enclosing copy of a resolu- tion regarding the affairs of Bulgaria." _ .

THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS.—The Executive Committee of the Liberal Unionist Association met on Wednesday in Lon- don, under the presidency of Lord Hartington, and deter- mined to hold a conference in the Metropolis about the end of the first week in December. Mr. Goschen, Sir H. James, Lord E. Cavendish, Lord &Abridge, Mr. H. Brand. Mr. E. Elliot, Sir F. Hobhoule, Mr. Craig-Sellar, Mr. R. B. Find- lay. Mr. Biddulph, and Sir R. Blennerhassett were present. Before the meeting Sir H. James had a private interview with Lord Hartington at Devonshire House. THE CHURCH nOUSE.—ThA result of the voting for ten representatives of the diocese of London in the House of Laymen. on Saturday, was declared. There were 22 candi- dates, and the result is a victory for the Evangelical party. In the last house there were eight High Churchmen and two Evangelicals, and in the present house the numbers are five and five. Lord Halifax (president of the English Union), Mr. Charles Powell (secretary of the Church of England Working-men's Society). Sir Walter Phillimore, and Colonel Makins, M.P., were among the candidates who failed to

• . secure election. SERIOUS GAS EXPLOSION AT ELUL LATIMM'S EESI- DENCH.—About two o'clock en Tuesday afternoon an ex- plosion of gas took place at 41, Portland-place, the residence of the Earl of Lathorn. The family arc, absent from home, and the house is in the care of the servants. A woman was

severely burnt about the head, and a man servant sue- tamed serious injuries to the face and hands. So great was the cencnssion that all the windows in the front of the house, from the basement to the roof, were burst outward. The walls of the hall and the adjoining rooms were much scorched, and the furniture was wrecked. ANOTHER GREAT FIRE AT THE LIVERPOOL DOCIIS.— Another fire of a serious and alarming character was dis- covered shortly after nine o'clock, Sunday morning, in one of the large cotton sheds at the Wellington Docks, Liver- pool. The shed, which is built on the north side of the dock, was filled with many hundredA of bales of cotton. The engines were at once got into play on the burning mass, but before complete mastery could be obtained over the fire, the lone range of rooting over the shed fell in. The fire was got under by noon, but the huge shed was then completely gutted, and its valuable contents damaged. The damage is estimated at from £30,000 to £40,000, probably covered by insurance. WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.—The annual meeting of the sup- porters of the National Society for Women's Suffrage was , held on Wednesday, in the Town Hall, Manchester. The Mayor of Manchester (Mr. Alderman Philip Goldschmidt) pre-sided, and addresses were delivered by Mr. W. Woodall, M.P., Mr. J. Addison, Q C., M.P., Mrs. Fawcett, and others. The report and statement of accounts for the rear were adopted and ordered to be printed and circulated, and the committee for the ensuing year were appointed. A resolu- tion was passed expressing satisfaction that Mr. Woodall has consented to again take charge of the Parliamentary Franchise (Extension to Women) Bill, and assuring him of support in such action as he may find it desirable to take with a view to bringing the question before Parliament on the earliest practical date next session. LORD ROSEBERY AND IMPERIAL FEDERATION. Lord Roseberv, in a manifesto signed by him as chairman of the Imperial Federation League, says the movement towards a federation of the empire has lately received an impulse and reached a stage which deserves serious attention and re- newed efforts on the part of the league. He says :—" Our policy has now for the first time been officially recognised by the Government of this country, which has publicly the suggestion urged upon it last August. We venture, therefore, to express an earnest hope that members of the league will use every effort to obtain from the Government, the Legislature, and the Press in their various colosies, careful consideration and hearty co-operation for the pro- posals which are to be made by the Imperial Govern- ment in accordance with the announcement in the Queen's Speech." BREAK EP OP A DESPERATE GANG OF BunGLarts.—The I Judge (Mr. Justice Wills) sat early on Saturday morning at ' Chester Assizes to try the remaining case and get away to Cardiff. It was one in which six men, named Parker,Moss, Hyde Bridge, Lynch, and Davies were charged with commit- ting a series of burglaries at Macclesfield; and John Crow- der, publican, was charged with receiving the stolen goods. The prisoners formed a gang who were the terror of the neighbourhood. Disguised with masks and armed with bludgeons and chisels, they perpetrated four burglaries in succession, stealing sums of money in silver and silver plate. Most of the property was found in Crowder's house. Lynch and Davies were found not guilty. Crowder was sentenced , to eighteen months', Mess to six and a half years' penal , servitude, and Parker, Hyde, and Bridge to eight years' penal servitude.

AN old writer says a frail woman is never so happy as when she discovers that another of her sex, hitherto regarded as above re- proach, has fallen from the path of virtue. The sage might have gone a little further and added that a feeling akin to this is not con- fined to the weaker vessel. We have evi- dence of this in an incident which has hap- pened in our midst. Our readers will remem- ber that, some six months ago, we convicted our contemporary the "Warrington Obser- ver," of procuring his leading articles by taking them from the "Sheffield Daily Telegraph." We say convicted, because, although the charge was publicly made and opportunity given for refuting.it, from that day to this the culprit has not had a word to say on the subject, and judgment has, there- fore, gone against him by default. His pun- ishment, as we can well understand, has been hard to bear, but people who take to stealing, whether in a literal or literary way, must ex- pect to suffer—when they are caught. The editor of " the recognised organ of the Con- servative party" has had to "grin and bide" —as the Lancashite phrase is—until last week, when he alighted on something which led him to conclude not only that there was another sinner as great as he, but that this particular sinner was the very person who had made public his own iniquity. Oh joy! what could be more fortunate! It is thus, thought he, that "the whirligig of Time brings in his revenges ; " and the frail one displayed some- thing of savage satisfaction in seeking to prove that another local editor had taken "a leading article from another paper and en- deavoured to palm it off as his own." We do not complain of this; it was quite natural under the circumstances. Indeed we will go so far as to say that, on the face of the evi- dence given, there was nothing for it but to conclude that the editor of this journal had been caught in the act of robbing another journal to supply the leading columns of his own paper. In order that our readers who do not see the "Observer "—there are very few copies to be seen—may perceive that we have no desire to shirk the charge against us, we may state, that in the last issue of our contemporary,, side by side with a leader which appeared in this journal on October 23rd, there was printed a leader which was found in the columns of the " Eastern Morning News," of October zoth that is three days earlier. The inference, in the ab- sence of any explanation, is that the "Examiner "leader had been taken from the "Eastern Morning News," and reprinted without acknowledgment, and this inference our contemporary did not fail to draw. The charge against us is distinct, and, as it is as grave as it is distinct, we must clear ourselves of it, or submit it to be a by- word and a reproach to all honest men. To begin with, we must say that so far from having been guilty of leader stealing from the "Eastern Morning News," we have not at any time seen that journal, nor did we know that the leader in'question had appeared in that paper until re saw the statement of our contemporary on Saturday last.
