then, it will be asked, is the extraordinary coincidence to be accounted for? The ex- planation is simple—that leader (and some others) was supplied to us by the same Lon- don agency which furnished that, -nd possi- bly other leaders, to the "Eastern Morning News." • And this brings us ter anothet• point of a personal kind which we should not otherwise have cared to allude to. The editor of our Tory contemporary measuring, it may be, a peck out of his own sack, meanly insinu- ates that he had had "serious doubts as to the authorship of the leading articles in the Examiner,' which," it is added, "have been altogether of a different style to the Touch and Go' matter." This is meant to suggest that the present editor of the "Examiner" has not been the writer of ti.e various lead- ing articles that have appeared in its columns since he took charge of the paper over two years since—that, in fact, a species of literary theft has been going on all the time. The present writer can afford to smile at the ridiculous suggestion. A serious illness which, seven weeks ago, incapacitated himH from work, necessitated a supply of leaders being obtained, for several weeks, from a London Press agency. Through some mis- understanding, leader matter was sent us which was written for daily papers like the "Eastern Morning News," whereas the articles we desired were such as would be furnished to the weekly journals doing business with the Agency in question. Previous, however, to this breakdown in health, the Editor of this journal had written every line which has appeared in its leading columns since the time of his appointmeDtto the post. More than that, so far from being'', a novice, he can say that for ten years up to ! September last, he had writt--n, on an aver- age three leaders or leaderettes each week without the break of a single week either for illness on holidays, thus making a total for I the decade of no less than 1,560 leading! articles. !When the critic who converts para. I graphs of Letters from London Correspon- dents into leaderettes, and wlio takes, or did 'take, his leading articles from the columns of the "Sheffield Daily Telegraph," can show as good a record of editorial work he may by that time have reached the conclusion that there are different styles for different subjects. Meantime it would be well for him to hide his diminished head; and since he will talk about the lion, let us commend Shakespere to him : Thou wear a lion's hide! doff it for shame, And hang a call's skin on those recreant limbs.

LIBERALS throughout the country have every reason to be gratified with the proceed- ings of the great Liberal Conference which was held at Leeds on Wednesday. It was a thoroughly representative body; it was de- liberative in its action; and unanimous in its conclusions. It might have been supposed, ' from the split in the party, and the disastrous results of the last General Election as a con- sequence of that split, that there would be some sign of dissatisfaction or discourage- ment in a Conference of this kind. But quite the reverse; the tone was determined; the utmost enthusiasm was manifested; and everything went indeed to show that the lead- ing Liberals of the Kingdom are in good heart. It would be absurd, of course, to say that any pleasure is taken in the fact that Dissentient Liberals like Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN still hold aloof from the main body of th... party; but it is some- thing that the course is made clear so far as dealing with Ole Liberal Unionists is con- cerned. Home Rule for Ireland is now accepted as the first article in the Liberal Programme ; and by that is meant "an Irish Legislative body for the management of what Parliament shall decide to be distinctly Irish affairs." If the Liberal Unionists in their de- sire to give local self-government for Ireland can bring themselves to recognise this basis of settlement of the Irish question, there is no reason why there should not be a speedy re-union of the Liberal party. If, on the other hand, they are still deter- mined as a section to halt by the way, the party as a whole is equally determined to march on without them. Progress, not retrogression, is the law of being, and when four-fifths of the Liberal party in England have declared in favour of Home Rule—with Ireland, Scotland, and Wales emphatically endorsing the verdict—it is in the nature of things impossible for the Legislature to stop short of Home Rule. It may be that legis- lative autonomy for Ireland will be denied for a time, and that a good deal of patience as well as perseverance will have to be exer- cised. The Liberal Unionists are for the most part a dogged set of men; and, so long as they find an unprincipled CHURCHILL at the head of affairs ready to do their bidding at the price of being kept in office, they will not be without inducement to pursue their present course. They will feel that if they are not themselves in office they are in reality in power; for has not the CHANCEL- LOR of the EXCHEQUER said in effect that he will do anything to preserve tile union with the Unionists? Mr. JOHN M-ORLEY treated with just contempt this unscrupulous declara- tion of Lord RANDOLPH exuRcHILL when he remarked, at the Leeds meeting, that if such evolutions were politics he would rather be a highwayman than a politician. There was another point which Mr. MORLEY Made which is worthy of special attention. He said : There is a combination to-day of men who agree in nothing so much as that Her Majesty would be graciously pleased to remove from her counsels for ever a Minister as great as Sir Robert Walpole. (Loud cheers.) We are all for union, but with those who are in that state of mind we cannot con- sent t 3 argue. (Cheers.) We will make no terms with them. We are not here to choose. a leader; there is no vacancy. (Loud and prolonged cheer- ing, the audience rising en inasse and enthusiastical- ly singing the strains of a political song, the re- frain of which was in honour of the "Grand Old Man.") Time has chosen our leader—years of de- voted service, not alone to his country but to the great cause of freedom all over the world. (Cheers.) 1 These are some of his titles to-day, and they are the titles to our allegiance which to-day's events have 1 written in large letters which no man can pretend to mistake, for he has a kingdom, not in Yorkshire only, of allegiance unbroken, of loyalty un- 4uenched, and of gratitude that time will not dim. Che3rs.) We are glad to note that the audience rose to the occasion in the enthusiasm it displayed in still looking to Mr. GLADSTONE :as the leader of the Liberal party. There is undoubtedly a disposition on the part of the Liberal Unionists—and some of them do not hesitate to avow it—to keen Mr. GLADSTONE out of office and to drive him from public life. They eierish the theory that if Mr. GLADSTONE were off the scene the Home Rule movement would instantly collapse. It is a delusion; but it is a delusion which they have hitherto hugged, though how they will be able to cling to it after such a demonstration as that of Wednesday last, it is difficult to say. Let these short-sighted, cold-blooded Liberals have it brought home to them then, first, that Home Rule for Ireland is the cardinal doc-

trine of the Liberal i'reed, and, second, that there can be no vacancy in the leadership of the party so long as Mr. GLADSTONE lives and is willing to hold the post which he has con- secrated by a thousand noble deeds. Let them fully realise this ; they will then see that they are fighting against fate, and at the eleventh hour they will, perhaps, "Conic over and help us" to do justice to Ireland.

"TOUCH AND GO." Working men generally would do well to follow the example of the St. Helens Trades Council in the effort they are making to strengthen their stakes and lengthen their cords. There is strength in union as well
as onion.

Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., addressed the St. Helens Trades Council the other evening, and repeated the hackneyed phrase that the interests of employer and employed are identical. And so they are in so far as they combine to seek a return—the one for capital and the other for labour. When it comes to the crucial question of apportioning the re- turn, the imerests of employer and employed are not identical; they are diametrically op- posed.

There seems to have been gross perjury in connection with the hearing of a case of as- sault at the Wallington Police Court on Mon- day morning. The Mayor said cne of the witness .7 deserved committing for trial. Why not p ceed in such a case ? It is the duty of magistrates to administer the law ; and when a culprit deserves punishment they should "let him have it."

The London Socialists, are, it seems, discreet as well as valorous. They will not, after all, tag themselves to the tail of the Lord Mayor's Show. They have decided not "to take the responsibility of leading an unarmed and defenceless people against a powerful body of armed men." Of course not—why shou'd they? But why didn't they think of that before?

The Vegetarians have " scored" at the Liverpool Exhibition, having furnished meals to no less than 130,000 people. This is a feather in Vac cap of our townsmen Mr. W. H. Chapman, who is superintendent of the restaurant on behalf of the Vegetarian Society. Medical authorities are agreed in saying we English people eat too much ani- mal food; we should be better if we were, say, half-bred Vegetarians.

If George Gerard had been a Vegetarian he wouldn't !lave lost his liberty. He has had to give an account of himself before the Warrington magistrates for stealing meat all hot, and, after despatching it, re- turning to purloin meat quite cold. He seems, from the description of the Chief Constable, to be, like Cardinal Wolsey, a man of "an unbounded stomach." But he will have to rein in ; he has been sent for three months to a place where hot meat will not trouble him, and where cold meat is un- known.

We like the Toryism of Sir Michael Hicks- Beach; there is so much old-time genuine stupidity about it. Addressing a meeting of the Fairfield branch of the Primrose League on Saturday, he advised those present, if they should visit Ireland, not to believe more than half they saw there. and not to believe any- thing they might hear. There now—that's the way to pursue an inquiry! Shut your eyes and open your mouth, and see what Beach will send you. -- Lord Egerton of Tatton would appear to be anticipating forthcoming legislation. His Cheshire tenants have received a circular in- forming them that in future his lordship will pay the tithe rent charges, which will be added to the rent and be payable therewith This is better than fighting a battle over each item of tithe rent. It protects the parsons too, for a time ; but the day is not far distant when the whole question of Church endow- ments, tithe included, will be settled on a new , footing.

It is a bad thing to sell bad meat, however profitable it may prove. But is is not always profitable, as Mr. Francis Lawrinson has found to his sorrow. On Monday, at Run- corn, he was fined Lzo, and over Lu in costs, for exposing for sale in his shop meat which was unfit for food, and for having..on his premises twenty pieces of meat of a simi- lar kina. It is satisfactory to see that the mapistrates in this case have imposed a heavy penalty. Butchers of questionable reputation require to be convinced that it doesn't pay to deal in questionable meat.

' Our neutral contemporary for Monday even - ing contains "A Young Man's Holiday," speci- ally written for the paper by, it may be presumed, a very young man who is very funny without being conscious of it. He tells of the girls who " wear their dresses a little below their knees," and then he goes on to say—" On Nancy we found several very larg e mushrooms."' This is altogether ' too funny- If he had found a thimble, or a hairpin; or a piece of ribbon, or a love letter, we could have understood it; but mushrooms !—really th II young man must be

Happy Glossop ! An offer of £2,000 to the town towards the erection of some public building has been increased to 1-..000 on the understanding that the scheme shall include a free library. Besides this, the town is to have an hospital at a cost of £25,000, the gift of Mr. Daniel Wood, and also public baths, which Mr. Samuel Wood has offered to build. It is hoped this will be " catching " as to Warrington. There are a dozen men in the town who could make out a cheque which would free the Warrington Lending Library. They wonld feel none the worse for it, and Warrington would be all the better.

Tir ESTABLISTMENT AND P.ROTESTANTISM.— Canon Taylor says Disestablishment is, I think, before us—as soon fIS the Irish question is settled. The Liberation Society's plan is to leave each clergy- man free to enter into any combination with others he prefers. So there would be nothing to prevent us at once forming a thoroughly Protestant Episco- pal Church, with Revised Book of Common Prayer and Protestant Bishops." Here, it will be seen, Canon Taylor fixes upon the suggestion which the Bishop of Oxford, and others of High Church lean- ings, have so unreasonably condemned, that, in the disestablishment of the English Church, there ' should not, as was the case in the Irish Church Act, 'be any legal compulsio.n placed upon its members to reunite themselves into a single body. Canon Taylor sees clearly enough that there is no real community of principle or purpose between the Evangelical and the sac.erdotal parties in tile Church of England, and, in the interests o 2 Pro- testantism, he is apparently not only prepared to welcome disestablishment, but to welcome it on the lines suggested by the Liberation Society. The Liberator. TRY LAWLESS'S Real some Made Damsons, 21b. jar, 6d. Market-place, Warrington.—Advt•

LOCAL NEWS.

WIDNES C.E.T.S.—Under the auspices of the society a lecture was delivered on Thursday evening by Captain W. C. Green, of Great Crosby. '1 he vicar presided. CAMDEN BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.—Mr. W. J. Shore presided over a c tpital entertainment held in Camden Schoolroom on Monday night. An attractive feature was the performance of The flower queen "by thirteen girls. Vi'ESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, RUNCORN.—The annual sermons' will be preached in St. Paul's Chapel, on Sunday. The annual meeting will be held on Monday evening at the same place. Full particulars in our advertising Columns. RIGBY CHARITY, RUNCORN.—Under the conditions of the will of the late Mr. Josiah Rigby, 62 widows were each presented at the Parish Church, Runcoro, on Monday night, with a flannel petticoat. The gifts were made at the close of the eervice held in celebration of the festival of All Saints. LACROSSE.— Widnes (A Team) v. Liverpool (3).—Played at Hough Green on saturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by five goals to two. Each team played only ten men. Widnes, who ware fairly represented, showed better form than they have done so far this season, scoring two goals in the first five minutes. Afterwards the game was more even, the home team obtaining three goals to two. Hough and the brothers Morgan did well for Liver- pool, while Gossage, Wylde, and Longtou played best for Widnes. ILLEGAL USE OF WATErt AT WIDNES. Mr. Benjamin Brown, a member of the Widnes Local Board, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge against the Widnes Foundry Co., in which he is a partner, of illegally using water.—Mr. Allen, clerk to the Board, said the case was not a very serious one, and Mr. Brown had promised that the offence should not be repeated at the works. It appeared that within the works is a house, ar d that the water supply thereto was utilised for making mor- tar to carry out a few repairs. A fine of 2s Gd and costs was imposed. WEST BANK BOARD SCHOOLS, WIDNES.—The Government report, just received, shows that the above schools have gained three " excellents," viz., the senior boys,' junior boys,' and junior girls' departments, the per centage of passes averaging over 97. This is the fourth time the senior boys' department has obtained the " excellent." It has also the highest per centage of the senior departments under the Board, and has earned the-highest sum on the average, viz 2e 64 per head. The three pupil teachers have again Passed excellent. The abeYo reti,cts great credit on the head master, Mr. J. S. Snoddy. - WESLEYAN FOREIGN MIsSIONS, WlDNES.—Dilring the past week, meetings have been held at Farnworth and pit- ton in aid of the above. Mr. F. Lewrinson presided over the Farnwerth meeting, held on Tuesday, and addresses were given by the Rev. R. Burden (Wesleyan), the Rev. R. Yeatman (Baptist), and Messrs. B. Brown and T. Robinson. Mr. Brown presided at the Ditton Meeting, when similar ad- dresses to those at Farnworth were delivered. The meetings at bath places were well attended, and the collections were eminently satisfactory. Services were held at each place on Sunday for the same object. HONOURS FOR A NATIVE OF RUNCORN.—The Bishop of London has aupointed to the Church of All :4aints', M ar- garet-s?reet, London, where the Prince and Princess of Wales are frequent worshippers, the Rev. W. Allen Whitwortn. Old Runcornians will remember that this clergyman is the son of a former incumbent of Holy Trinity Church, Run- corn, and that the whole of his early life was passed in Run- corn. The Bishop of London is very slow in filling up livinzs in his gift, and All Saints would in ten days have lapsed to the Primate, but he has certainly made a wise choiee in Mr. Whitworth, who is one of the few Liberal cicrgy in the metropolis. A LONG STRUGGLE AT WIDNES. Bernard Cullen, a labourer, appeared before the Widnes magistratee on Mon- day to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Cromwell-street, and also with assaulting P.C. Houghton. On Saturday night the officer took Cullen into custody on the first cnarge. Cullen resented his arrest by st.iking the officer to the ground by a blow on the chest, and then kicked him. Constable Worsfold went to his comrades aid, and a struggle of 20 minutes duration ensued before they could place the handcuffs en the prisoner. A total tine of 15s and costs was imposed upon the prisoner, who had been five times previously before the Bench. RESCUE FROM DROWNING BY A RUNCORN MAN.—At the County Police Court at Manchester, on Saturday, a woman named Hann 41 Mayers (30), wife of a man living at Clif- ford-street, Old Tra.ffoid, was charged with attempting sui- cide by jumping into the Bridgewater canal at Stretford, on tbe previous morning. From the evidence, it appeared that prisoaer was seen by a boatman named William Bolton, of Runcorn, to jump into the canel near Longford Bridge at Stretford. Bolton jumped in after her, and, with assistance, drew her from the water. She asked not to be taken out. Bolton gave information to the police, and she was given into custody. The maeistrates let her go, WIDNES AND RUNCORN FOOTBALL TEAMS. -- The Com- mittee of the Runcorn Football Club have decided not to play the return match at Widnes 014 December 4th, but to forward insteed a checiee for half the gate received on Sat- urday last. We understand that the reason for this decision is the strong feeling displayed amongst the townsfolk on both sides of the river, and also the allegation that the Wid- nes team played "rough." While in Runcorn this decision is applauded, in Widnes it has given rise to great derision, and the popelar impression is that fear of sustaining a re- veres is the motive for cancelling the engagement. It was thought that the differences that existed between the clubs for so many years were healed up, but the breach is now wirl- r than ever. FARNWORTH VICARAGE.—The winter session in connec- tie i with the Farnworth C.E.T.S. was commenced on Tues- day night, when a capital programme, consisting chiefly of recitations and dialogues, was gone through in the National Schools. The Vicar (the Rev. George Bond) presided. and in the course of his remarks stated that he had received that ' evening a communication from King's College, Cambridge, that, in answer to a petition from the four church wardens of Farnworth, they had resolved to hand over £lO2 per annum of theavicerage tithe, now paid to Prescot. to the Vicaraae of Farnwerth, in consideration of the great extent of the parish, the large amount of tithe paid by it, and the fact that Farnworth itself is directly under the patronage of King's College, being the gift of the Vicar of Piescot. ( • pplause.) A FIGHTING BUTCHER AT WIDE CS —Lawrence Tim- mins, butcher, Liverpool, appeared at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly, and also of apsaulting P.C. Strong and damag- ing the uniform of P.C, Luther Thompson. On Monday I night, at closing time, the defendant and several men and women emerged from the Grosvenor Hotel, in Victoria- road. One of the females discovered that she had left an article behind, and the party appealed to P.C. Strong to gain their admission. He stated his inability to oblige them, when the defendant pulled off his coat, seized the officer by the collar, and struck him on the chest. P.C. Thompson came up to aid in the apprehension, and the defendant, in his violent struggles, tore that officer's trousers. The de- fendant had to pay a total sum of 15s 93, or go to gaol for 21 days' hard labour. ACCIDENTS AT -WIDNES.—Joseph Oilier, seven years of age, was walking along the boundary wall at Appleton Quarry, on Monday afternoon, when he slipped and fell a distance of about 30 feet. He is suffering from three severe scalp wounds, and several of his ribs are fractured. The boy, whose home is at Manchester, is on a visit to 44, Kent- street, Widnes.—A youth named Hudson, empleved at the Widnes Foundry, was on Tuesday morning steadying a box which was being hoisted by a crane, when the chain slipped. The falling box struck Hudson to the ground and severely injared his ankle and head. Hudson lives in Carleton- terrace, Milton-road, Widnes.—An old man named William Harrison was run over in Victoria-road by a cart belonging to Tae)ock Brewery Company. He was stepping from the roadway on to the parapet when he fell, and the wheels of the vehicle passed over him. His right arm and leg were seriously fractured.—On Tuesday Wm. Kenyon, of South- street, Widnes, who is a boilermaker at Widnes Foundry, had his head split open by the handle of a travelling crane. He is under the care of Dr. McLennan. THE RECF.NT ORANGE DISTURBANCES AT WIDNES.—In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tharsday, Mr. Little ap- plied ex parte for a mandamus calling upon the justices of Widnes, to bring up certain recognisances, in order that they might he quashed.—Learnad counsel stated that on the 14th August last one Wainwright and several other persons were engaged in a procession through the streets of Widnes, accempanied by a band, which, it was alleged, played a party tune. This resulted in a disturbence, and the men for whom he appeared were charged before the magistrates with committing 'a breach of the peace by marching along certain streets with a band of music playing a party tune,l brandishing sticks and making a great noise, and alarming divers subj,Cts of our Sovereign Majesty the Queen." While admitting that there was evidence that the parties had marched through the streets with a band playing a party tune, the learned counsel submitted that there was no evidence of a breach of the peace. Notwithstandine the absence of evidence of disturbances, his clients were bound ever in their own recognisences to keep the peace for six months.—Their lordships, after a short discussion, granted a rule nisi. A VACCINATION CASE AT RUNCORN.—At Rnncorn Police Court on Monday, Thomas Harrison, keeper of the Stanley Arms, High-street, was charged with having neglected to have one of his children, named Alfred Harrison, vaccinated within three months after its birth. and not rendering a reasonable excuse for the neglect.—Mr. Henry Coleburn, the vaccination officer, proved serving the usual notices upon the defendant, and also with calling at the house respecting the matter. The defendant had alleged that the child was too unwell to be vaccinated, but both he and his wife had neglected to get the necessary medical certificate. —The defendant pointed out that the child was vaccinated on the 25th October, and the summons was taken out on the 27th. It was impossible, he said, to get a certificate of successful vaccination until after the expiration of seven days. He alleged that the proceedings had been taken by Mr. Coleburn from spleen. He bad reared a family of twelve children, and after his experience he thought he was the best judge of the fitness of his children for vaccination. —Mr. H. Reynolds said it the child was unwell it was the defendant' duty to get a medical certificate in order that the vaccination might be postponed.—The defendant ad- mitted that he had never read the instructions on the notices.—Mr. Coleburn denied that any feeling had been shown. He had been vaccination officer for more than thirty years, and this was only the second case he had had to take, eo that it could not be said he had acted in bad feeling.— The Bench imposed a fine of 2. 64 and costs, and informed Mr. Coleburn that he had done his duty.

THE ANTI-VACCINATION QUESTION AT EARLES- TOWN.—At the Petty Sessions, at Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, four parents, named Charles Kelly, Joseph Blakemore, Arthur Wolfenden, and Edward Dickens were summoned for not comply- ing with the law by refusing to have their chil- dren vaccinated. The cases were proved by Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer. All the defendants most emphatically refused to have their children vaccinated. Kelly said that be had seen the conse- quences of the practice in his own family ; he had had two brothers crippled through it, and should not allow his child to be vaccinated. Mrs Blake- more expressed the same determination, saying that her conscience, and that of her husband, would not allow them to have their baby vaccinated. Wolfen- den asked the magistrates to define the meaning of . vaccination. "What," l4e desired to know, "does the law mean by saying that I must have it vacci- nated?" The presiding magistrate, Mr. R. Hough- ton, intimated that it was pretty well understood what the law was on that subject. The wife of Dickens complained that as she had a large family and her means were narrow, it was not right that she should have been summoned, while others in a better position were passed over. Finally, how- ever, she said that she would rather part with her bed than have her children vaccinated. A fine of as and costs was imposed on each defendant. CLAIM AGAINST A RAILWAY COMPANY.—On Thursday, at the Warrington County Court, an ac- tion was heard before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, in which Albert Broom, farmer, of Preston Brook, sued the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany for the value of a lamb alleged to have been killed in consequence of the company's line being improperly fenced. Mr. Preston, jun. (Liverpool)'', appeared for the defence.—Plaintiff, who conducted his own case, said that he had a flock of 50 sheep and 76 lambs in a field belonging to him in May last, and alleged that owing to the poor condition of the fence, which the Railway Company were bound to repair, one of the best lambs of the flock got on to the railway and we 6 killed, and was afterwards taken on to Warrington. The amount claimed was ss. Plaintiff contended that the Railway Com- pany were bound by law to fence their property against the trespass of sheep or cattle.—Mr. Pres- ton said there was no evidence as to the condition of the fence. He also pointed out that what evi- dence the plaintiff had given was only hearsay.— Plaintiff was cross-examined, and stated that the flock of sheep and lambs was feeding near to the railway. It was possible that the sheep might have got on the Northwich-road, and passed along the road which went to- wards an adjoining field, which was oc- cupied by Mr. Lightfoot, or it might have got on to the towing path of the North Staf- fordshire Company's .canal, and thence on to the railway. Mr. Lightfoot had no fence to his field, which was hounded on one side by the Thvilv,ray Company's line, and on the other by the canal. The Railway Company's fence was in a poor condition. —Mr. Preston said the defence was that plaintiff's fence was in poor condition, and that the sheep and lambs strayed, and after ci.etting on the Canal Com- pany's premises and through Mr. Light foot's field, trespassed on to the railway. About six o'clock on the morning in question a number of plaintiff's sheep were seen on the line by Richard High field, a foreman platelayer in the employ of the Railway Company. Highfield saw the carcase of a lamb on an engine, and was informed that it had been run over. He drove the remainder of the sheep off the line, and they got into plaintiff's field through gaps in the fence.—His Honour said that plaintiff could not recover, as he had not brought sufficient evi- dence. He gave judgment for the defendant com- pany with costs.

SHOCKING DEATH OF A BUTCHER.—A frightful accident occurred at Golborne early on Saturday Morning, when an assistant.butcher named James Stirrup, aged 29, nearly severed 'one leg from his bOdy. The poor fellow was in the act of cutting the hind quarter of a cow when -the knife slipped and plunged into his thigh to the depth of several inches, completely severing the femoral artery. He was immediately attended by a doctor, but was almost lifeless in a few minutes from loss of blood, and death ensued within half an hour.—On Monday Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at Gcilborne upon the bod; ot the deceased. The principal wit- ness was Thomas Connor? butcher, Wigan, who said deceased and he were in their shop in High-street, Golborne, at the time named. Deceased called out, "Oh, Tom, I've cut my leg," and shortly afterwards dropped to the ground. Lige was taken to the doc- tor's, and everything doff to save him, but with- out avail, the femoral artery being severed. Wit- ness added that deceased, who was very powerful, was slashing through the hind quarter of a cow, drawing the knife towards him, when it slipped and 'plunged into his leg. A verdict of "Accidental death " was returned, - BETTING PROSECUTIONS AT WARRINGTON.—At Warrington Borough Court,' on Thursday morning, before Major Litton and Alderman Webster, John Monks was summoned that he, being the occupier of the house 4, Ship-yard, had on certain dates al- lowed it to be used for the purpose of betting on horse race's. John Mather and John James Mather, Golden-street, were summoned for using the house for the purposes of betting. The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. J. L. Whittle), wito appeared to prose- cute, said that he understood that the defendants were anxious. that the cases should be adjourned, as their solicitor was not able to attend that day. He had no objection to that course being taken, on con- dition that the costs were paid by the defendants. Defendant Mather, senior, said that they had not had sufficient time to prepare their defence. The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. White) said that the Costs amounted to 12s Gd. Defendant Mather: Ido not think I have got it with me. Will they take my hat for it? Chief Constable Hunt: The fees of the court should be paid now. Defendant Mather: I should think you could trust a respectable man like me for twelve 'hours. The cases were then ad- journed for a fortnight, as were also summons?s taken out against Henry Gittens, of the Swan Inn, Bridge-street, and Elizabeth Butterworth and Seven Stirrup, ,of, the Ram's Head Inn, Horse- market-street.
NEW BAPtIST CHAPEL FOE WIDNES. SL s OF WORE. _

'With the object of adding to the fund which has for I its purpose the erection of a new Baptist Chapel at Wid- nes, a rale of work was commenced in the Baths essembly Foom on Tueeday. The present chapel is obscured amid a number of dingy tenements in a back street, whilst the atmosphere of the neighbourhood is of the Most disagree- able nature, through the proximity of several chemical works. Mr. Spurgeon, ef the London Tabernacle, has written a characteristic letter (published in last week's Examiner", commending the cauee, and speaking highly of Mr. Yeatcnan's services during his three years' residence in Widnes. The site of the proposed new chapel is at the corner of Lugedale-road, partly facing the new Public Offices and St. Paul's Church, and will be a most con- venient and admirable fr;tuation. Amongst those present at the eeening ceremony were the Revs. H. Yeatman (pastor), Re Bunion (Wesleyan), J. Beyeant (Wesleyan). te. Hugees (Coneregationat), and Hugh Owen (Welsh Wes- leyan) ; Messrs. R. Shew, S. Owens, F. H. Penkhurst, and others. A hymn haying been sung. the Rev. It. Burdon read the Scriptures, and the Rev. J. Bryant offered up ' prayer. The Rev. R. Yeatman said the movement for the erection of a new Baptist chapel was cammenced about five years I ago, in this way. Seine ot the young men of the chapel , wart oat carol singing and gathered about £7, which formed 1 the nu !lens of the chapel fund. By sales of work, which 1 had ben increasingly successful, and subscriptions received i from. yell ms gentlemen, thissum had accumulated to £2.0, nearly the whole of which had been raised during his three I years.' pastorate amongst them. Then one or two of the friends rhoueht it would te a good plan if all connected with the pl.cd mould make a promise that they would give, within a year if poesible, a certain surer of money. In almost every iestance the promises were fulfilled. (Hear, bear.) He knew this cost their friends a good deal of self-denial, because, Ike some other °hut cbes in the town, they bat no , very wealthy people amongst them. (Hear, hear) This was the way in which tt.e money bad been raised. They i hid, however, made progress in another direction. They had practicaly secured a site for the proposed new chapel at;Andere-i.'s Coraerebut the matter could not be settled for about a month, as the Legh estate was in chancery: They hoped to raise sufficient money by that sale of work to make the trensfec of the land entire at once. (Applause.) He need not say anything about the necessity tnere was for a new chap-I, for those who knew the present chapel would know what a bad neighbourhood it was in, and would agree with him that no place of worship ought to be in such an out of the way place. (Hear, hear.) But besides these , disadvantages, it did not matter which way the wind blew, I they got a great deal of the smoke and gas of the surround- ing works, and suffering under these inconveniences they found that they could not make any headway. and that they must, if possible, get into a better neighbourhood. They were making the effort and hoped to be successful. (Ap- plause.) Mr. R. Shaw expressed his pleasure at being present. He should have felt very sorry indeed not to have been present, because he remembered that be had something to do with the erection of the present Baptist Chapel. When he came to Widnes that chapel did not exist. The Coneregationalists, with whom he was then associated ,worshipped at that time in that unsuitable building, the Public Hall, and he could tell them that they considered they had made a great stride when they got into the present Baptist Chapel. (Hear, hear.) After worshipping in that place for a considerable time, it was thought too small and inconvenient, and efforts were made to remove to a more commodious building in what was thought a better locality for a place of wursbip. Their efforts were crowned with abundant success. The discarded building then came into the possession of the 'Baptists, and he hoped their efforts would be crowned with a like success to that to which he had referred. (Hear, hear.) Great changes had taken place in that part of Widnes where the Baptists worshipped, and it was of groat I importance that they should move in the direction to which Mr. Yeatman had referred. He hoped they would get that help from the gentlemen of Widnes, who were always will- ing to help', forward a good cause. (Hear, hear.) Sometimes circumstances might prevent them from being as liberal as they could like to be. They were told on all hands that they were going tohave laetter trade, and if they had he felt satisfied that there a number of liberal minded men in Widnes who would come forward and help them as they had helped every good cause in the district. (Hear, hear.) Therefore they might take courage, and continue in the gocd work they had commenced. He hoped that in a few years they would have a splendid chapel where they could 'worship God with comfort and amid appropriate sur- roundings. The object they had in view was ene that must commend itself to the feelings and better judgment of all right-minded men, and he trusted they would be able to. open the new chapel, when erected, almost free from debt. Be wished them every success, and had much pleasure in declaring (hat the sale of work might commence. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. R. Yeatman in felicitous terms moved a cordial vote of thanks to Mr. Shaw for his services. He mentioned that Mr. E. K. Mnspratt had sent £5 towards the new chapel fund—(applause)—and many other persons had promised to assist them.
The Rev. Hugh Owens seconded, and the Rev. R. G. Hughes supported the motion, which was carried by accla- mation.

The fair vendors then commenced the sale of their wares. The stalls, five in number, were laden with an interesting collection of useful and fancy articles, and the room presen- ted an attractive appearance. Parcels of goods had been received from Mesdames Bennett, H Brunner, E Carey, Ed- wards, Hudson, Jones, Lomax, Rollason. and Hancock (Staffordshire) ; Misses Cooper, Holms (Manchester). and Marshall ; Messrs. J. 0. Jackson (Sutton). T Rigby (Fred- sham), T Smith, T S Swale, E Warhatn, Cressy (Manches- ter). and E Carey. The following were in charge of the various stalls :—Mes- dames Bennett, Bailey, Baker, Callon, J Davies, Hingley, Jones, Lomax, Robinson, Thompson, and Welling; Misses Bailey, H Bailey,iMacKereth, Moores, E Moores, J Passel', Rose Passey, Priestnall, Seddon, Thompson, J Thompson, Welling, and Wood. There was a good attendance in the evening, and amongst the amusements provided was a concert in which Miss Priestnall, Miss Sarah Coof (who received an encore), sung songs, and Miss Rose Passey performed a pianoforte solo ; while the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Isalc Edwards. sang several glees. The Rev. R. G. Hughes gave readings from Shakespeare, which were much enjoyed. The amount realised was £3O. The s.le was continued on Wednesday afternoon, when Mr. H. Brunner, of Appleton, performed the opening cere- mony. Amongst those present were the pastor (the Rev. R. Yeatman), and Revs. R. Burdon, J. Bryant, J. Calvert, and David Davies and Mr. E. Carey. After a few observations from Mr. Yeatman, Mr. Brunner delivered an address. Knowing, he said, the great amount of good Mr. Yeatman had done during his sojourn in Widnes, and sympathising most heartily with the object they had in view, he could not refuse to come and open that sale as requested. He thought they were quite right in corning out from the bad locality in which they were placed. It was certainly not right that they should hide their light under the bushel of a back street. He hoped they would be successful in raising the necessary amount of money, and that after establishing the new chapel that they would make all the progress that themselves or their minister could desire. He et-pressed his pleasure at the presence that day of the ministers of various denominations, and said they might have their religious differences, but he believed that when- ever people could they ought to meet together and assist one another. The ministers of all denominations were en.- gaged in doing good work, and when it was possible for
I laymen to show their sympathy with the work they should do so. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner then declared the proceed- ' ings opened._ _ _ . .
ihe-Rev. R. Yeatman moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Btunner for his kindness.

Mr. E. Carey seconded the motion. Referring to Mr. Brunnei's remarks, he said he had known Widnes longer than anyone in that room, end 11,3 had always found the people extremely willing to help each other in every possible way. and there was evidence of thegood feeling existing in the pre- aence of the ministers that day. Mr. Brunner had very long . been a near neighbour of his and a very valued friend, and ' if width of mind enabled a man to feel sympathy with every denomination, then that man was Mr. Brunner. (Applause.) He could assure Mr. Brunner that be had appeared there in a good cause. The Baptists had been hard at work in Wid- nes for many years, and to this he could testify—had worked with extreme self denial and extreme energy. Be Idid not think there was any denomination in the town that had worked harder in proportion to its nit arts and opportu- nities, and he was sure he, for one, would congratulate the Baptists most heartily when they succeeded in attaining ! the great object of their desire which they so much desired that was the new chapel at Anderson's corner. (App)ause.) The Rev. R. Burden anti the Rev. J. Bryant also spoke, and the inotiun was carriA by acclamation.

div.head: MED,CLL OFFICER.S FPORT.
div.p: MED,CLL OFFICER.S FPORT.

The Medical Officer reported that du lug the month of October there were 31 deaths registered. of which six were inquest cases. and represeetir..g etu atmual dean rate of 21 per 1,1100. Four deaths were due to bronchitis, three to diarr lima, and three to consumption. Recently he had ex- it novel method of ventilation that obtained in several ;_e.rts of the township. Tee down water spouts fixed to satire house were mule into sewer ventilators as well as water carriers. Oae end of the spout was fixed under the ledge of the building and the other was fixed to the sewer. There was no intervening trap. The sewer gas found a ready er,ress through the very imperfectly made joints of the pipes, and ingress into the dwellings through any near opening. It was not an uncommon tiling to Fee the,e spouts reared np in dangerously close proximity to day rooms as well as bedrooms. In many instances the roof end of the spent was dangerously too near the bedroom Itindows. He would strongly urge the Authority to pass A resolution requiring the diseJntina- auce of this highly risky teiethod ut sewer ventilation, as well as to require that all spouts that perform this dual function were altered without undue or needless delay. 11-3 ' regretted to iaform the Authority cf art outbreak of typhoid fever in a building situated on the south-end of the town that was used as a dwelling, and had been partly used as business premises. Everything was being 4one to localise the evil. A young person was also ill of typhoid fever at Peewit Hall. The sanitary surroundings were eminently of an unsatisfactory character. In front of the cottage there was a large pit within a fete yards of the that had been used for many years a 3 a cesspool for i reception of bedroom and other slops. There was a midden with a cesspool almost adjoining the cottage wall. The privy and ashpit arrant,ements were of the most primitive kind, and the water supply was of a most suspicious character. Samples had been forwarded to the county analyst. The well from which the cottagers get their supply of portable water during dry weather was in close proximity to the above mentioned pit ;ire rainy weather they got their water supply from a field close by.—ln reply to the Chairman, the Surveyor said there were a good I nanv down spouts connected with the sewers.—The Chair:nem : Thera you don't agree with the doctor in doing away with them ?—The Surveyor said spouts were always considered a very good outlet. They did not connect many now.—Mr. White said the sewers were never connected on that plan now.—The Medical Officer pointed out that Fewer gas in any dwelling was highly dangerous ; and when the bedroom windows were opened the gas would certainly enter into them in many instances. It was a dangerous method of ventilation, and ought to be discontinued at once. There had been for some time a number of scarlet fever symptoms ice places where one would have expected the sanitary arrangements to be of the most perfect character, and they might have some connec- tion with this system of ventilation.—The repert was referred to the Health Committee.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTrE.
div.p: THE GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTrE.

This committee recommended that lamps be purchased and fixed at the following places :—Eight pillar lamps in Norman-road, three bracket lamps in Okell-street, one bracket lamp in Porter-street, one bracket lamp at the lower end of Clarence-street, and that a lamp at the lower end of Waterloo-road be moved a- diso.oce of 12 vard:-..—Mr. Grice mov.el, and Mr. Hankinson seconded, the adoption of the minutes —Mr. Meadowcroft thought the Board ought to have some reasons given why that expenditure in Norman- road was proposed. There were only two houses in that road, there was practically no traffic of a public character, and its greatest use was by the young people who wished for an ev,ning's walk. (Laughter.)—Mr. Lake: Who prefer darkness rther than light. (t.aughter.)—Mr. Meadowcroft said there was a desire amongst some of the members that they should economise and keep down the rates, but thisl p-apesal would entail an annual expenditure of £l6, of which they would onl.e teceive £5 back in rates.—Mr. Shaw said it was strange that the chairman of this commit- tee had not thought it aeedful to give any information on the proposed large expenditure of £26 per annum. This was equivalent to expending £650 at 4 per cent., and he ' thought that if a member was to bring forward a resolution lasking the Board to spend £650. being a permanent charge upon the rates, they would want to know something of it. He alleged that the expenditure on the making of that road was illegal, but happily they had got out of that difficulty by the auditor passing it. He warned them teat if they carried out this proposition the Board would soon be in- volved in a heavy expenditure for paving, flagging, and sewering the road; and contended in addition that it was a good road to walk along at present, and needed no lights. He objected to the passing of the minutes.—ln consequence of this objection the discussion could not further proceed, and the matter will have to be considered at a special meet- ing next week.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY.

The minutes of the—Financa Coßimittee contained the following summary of receipts for the montb;—General dis- trict rate, £303 103 4d: market rents and tolls, £26 78 id; rent of offices (School Board), £l5; slaughter-houses £2 16a id; total £347 13s 6d. Accounts amounting to £222 Os 6d were recommended for payment by the various Committees. The Committee also recommended that the sanction of Her Majesty's Treasury be obtained to the borrowing of a sum not exceeding £lBO for the extension of premises of the Free Public Library.—Mr. Dobson moved the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. Mellor enquired for some further in- formation with reference to toe proposed alterations of the Public Library. He had heard it stated that the course resolved upon would mean throw- ing mor.ev away, and would spoil the building. IMr. Meadowcroft explained that it had been decided to en- large the library premises, because the accommodation in the reading room was inadrquate.—Mr. Meadovrcroft, on the suggestion ot the Law Clerk, substituted the following resolation: " That the approval of Her Majesty's Treasullir be obtainei to the appropriation for the purpose of the Pub- lic Library of a part of land and building at the Town Hall."—After some further conversation, Mr. Mellor raised an objection to the minutes, and it was referred to an ad- journed meeting of the Board

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The first meeting of the new Board was held on Thurs- day afternoon. Present : Revs. Father Clarke, Father Fine- gan, G. Bond, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Tiwinis, Bradshaw, Deacon, Wareing, Heyes, and G. E. Danhy (clerk), Mr. Danhv took the chair pro tens. APPOINTMENT OF CHAIIIMA.N.—Father Clarke said be had the pleasing duty to perform of asking them to vote to the ! chair a gentleman who was eminently possessed of the qualities of a good chairman. They might judge of a man by his acts, aud if they looked at the past conduct of the gentleman he was about to propose they would find that he had proved himself to be eminently qualified to be chairman of that Board. He meant Mr. Tit-rinds. (Applause.) He I had ruled that Board with firmness and kindness, and the actions of the Board as a rule bad the unanimous assent of the members. The few votes that were not unanimous had certainly not been the fault of the chairm tn. He bed the greatest confidence that Mr. Tirnmis would fulfil his duty in the future as he had done in the past, in a manner consistent with the dignity of the position be held. (Applause.)—Father Finegan seconded the motien with the greatest pleasure, and endorsed in the heartiest manner all that had beem said by Father Clarke. Mr. Tim- mis had the respect of every member of the Board—(hear, bear)—and althou:4ll he uould not make any promises for himself for the future—(Mr. Timmis : Be a good boy. Laughter.)—Lie could promise that Mr. Tirnmis would be all that Father Clarke had paintid him, and the most able to harmonise the different elements of the Board. (Applause.) —Mr. Imison supported the motion, as did the Rev. G. Bond, who said Mr. Tivamis was almost the only possible one that they could have to take the chair.—Father Finegan (shaking his head): No, no.—Mr. Timrais : Everyone of us could take the chair.—Rev. G. Bond (to Father Finegan) : There is no doubt you would fid a good big chair. (Langh- ter.) The uniform kindness and ability Mr. Timmis had displayed fully entltled him to take the chair. (Hear, hear.) _The proposition was carried unanimously —Mr. Tirnmis, who, on tikine, the chair was loudly applauded, said if he had consulted his own feelings be should hesitate about resuming this position, but after the unanimous rote, he could not hesitate. He therefore accepted the trust they had placed in his hands, and he thanked them all very cor- dially for the unanimous de,ire they had expressed. They knew the course he had taken in times past during the many years he had occupied the position and by their vote last week they were good enough to express approval of what he did, which he thought he might take as the best evi- dence of their appreciation, the unanimous vote they had passed that day. (Hear, bear.) He had always endeavoured to act fairly and impartially and with courtesy—(hear, hear)—and it would he his object to act in tbe future as he had done in the past. If he obtained from the Board the support he had received in former years he was quite sure the proceedings of the Board would be as unanimous as they had been hitherto. (Applause )—On the proposition of Mr. Deacon, seconded by the Rev. Geo. Bond, Mr. Brad- shaw was unanimously elected vice-cbairman.
TIME OF MEETIMG.—It was decided to hold the meeting of the Board on the third Tuesday in each month, at two o'clock in the afternoon.

THE COST OF Tits ELEcrtoN.—A letter was read from Mr. S. H. Hartley, the returning officer, informing the Board that the cost of the election was £lB6 18s 10d, and asking for a cheque for that sum.—The Chairman: It is a good big bill, zentlernen —Mr. Wareing : Amd there were big results, Mr. Chairman. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held yesterday morning at the Town Hall. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Handley, F. A. Lake, and E. Imison, with F. Rif;,bv (clerk). APPOINTMENT OF VICE-CHAIRMAN.—On the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Imison, Mr. R. Lea was appointed vice-chairman in place of Mr. Pritchard. The Clerk presented the annual statement of receipts and lexpenditure for the year ended the 29th September. The total receipts amounted to £2,611 14s 10, including a balance in hand of £1,349 93 9d, Government grants, £lll is 11d, and school fees £122 3s 3d. The pay- ments made to the Boqrd by the rating authori- ties at 41d in the £ was £l,OOO. The total expenditure was £2,525 163 101 The salaries of officials of the Board amounted to £204 15 80, and the legal and other expenses of administration £S4 Is. The salaries of teachers were £290 2s Si, books, apparatuo, and stationery cost £lO4 63, fuel, light, charring, replacement of furniture, repairs to building, &c., £l6O 18s 100. The sum of £1,077 17s 9d, was spent in the purchase of land and erection, and alteration of school buildings, whilst £260 was spent in furnishing the same. The sum of £307 ISs 7d had been repaid as principal and interest of loans.- The outstanding liabilities of the Board amounted to £5,163 17s 9d.—ln reply to questions the clerk stated that the sun of • about £2OO was spent in furniture, books, and in generally starting the schools in Greeuway-road, and in repairs at Mill Brow School. This amount had been paid out of the rates, as it could not be charged to capital account. The rate was considerably larger than it would have been, had the grants been better. The poor results could not be avoided by reason of the schools being opened in the middle of the school year—The statement was passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—Mr. Handley made a report with regard to the average attendance at each school during the month of October, and stated that there had been a sub- stantial increase in the attendance of every school, In Sep- tember the per centage of attendance was 73, this month the per centage was 79, showing an increase of 6 per cent. throughout the town. At the new Board school there had been a decrease of GO on the rolls during the past two months, probably because the novelty had worn off. A number of these had been stated to have gone to private ad- venture schools, but in a good number of the cases it had been found that the children were not in attendance at those schools, and were therefore presumably wandering about the streets. The Board had got a copy of the registers of four out of the five private adventure schools, but the fifth positively refused to allow them a copy. I There was no other business of public interest.

THE W.ABRINGTON HARRIERS.—These harriers had a cross-country run on Saturday, from the Bold. Arms Hotel, Bold. The hares, T. Gleave and H. Maddock, left with the bags at 3-30, the pack fol- lowing at 3-40, with J. Bowen acting as pace. R. Sherlock, G. Stokes, A. Ratcliffe, G. Ratcliffe, J. Monks, J. Bellian, and D. Walsh also ran, the last- named amting as whip. The trail lay along Liver- pool-road for about two and a half miles, then past the Red Lion' leaving Peck Hill to the right, and: along the road to Upton Quarry. Then it lay across the fields to Farnworth Church, and along the road' again. The hares arrived at 4-25, and the pack at 4-31, D. Walsh being first, R. Sherlock second, and. G. Ratcliffe third and the rest close up. The dis- tance was about eight miles. FREE LENDING LIBRARY.—A meeting of the committee which has been formed to carry on the' agitation in favour of making the Warrington Lending Library free to the public was held at the, Horsemarket-street Cocoa Rooms on Wednesday evening. Mr. Thomas Moths occupied the chair, land reported the result of the sending out of cir- culars dealing with the question. The bulk of the replies he had received were distinctly favourable to the course they were taking. The committee were, therefore, greatly encouraged in the work they had in hand. After some discussion, it was resolved that a meeting be called of the larger body of supporters for Thursday evening next, at the Horsemarket-street Cocoa Rooms, to take into con- sideration the advisability of requisitioning the ' Mayor to call a town's meeting upon the question. It was understood that all supporters of the move- : ment would be welcomed at the meeting.

VEGETARIANISM AT THE LIVERPOOL EXREBT.. TION.—On Saturday morning the Executive of the Vegetarian Society, together with various friends ot the movement, partook of breakfast in the- dining-room of the society at the Liverpool Exhi— bition. A meeting was afterwards held, under the. presidency of Ma,, W. E. A. Axon, for the purpose of thanking Messrs. E. Collkr and William Harri- son, of Glazebrook, near Warrington, for the hon - any assistance they had rendered towards making the dining-room a success. Mr. W. IL Chapman, Warrington: manager of the dining-room, in a state- ment snowing the number who had visited the re- staurant, stated that on the whole it had been more succcesful than the dining-room conducted under the society's auspices at the Health Exhibi- tion in 1884. The number of persons who had visi- ted the Liverpool dining-room and partaken of meals was 130,000. Brief addresses were after-' wards given. Duncan McLellan, labourer, died on Saturday morning from having tapped a cask of sheep-dip, on board the steamer Minard Castle, in Glasgow harbour, in the belief that it was- whiskey.

div.head: NE WT ON \ COM MIBSIONERS.
div.p: NE WT ON \ COM MIBSIONERS.

The monthly meeting of the Newton lmproyernent Corn- missionsrs was held on •Monday afternoon, when there were present Messrs. W. F. Gooch (chairman), T. J. Gillespie, J. W. Emmett, B. B. Glover, T. Forster, T. Hunt, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and R. Briefly (surveyor). TUB DISGIIIIACHFUL STATE 011' WARGRATE ROAM.

A special meeting of thd Highways, Pubhc Works, and Sanitary Sanitary Committee was held on the 4th tilt. The following is an extract from the minutes :—"The Law Clerk reported his interview with Mr. Pardey as to the making of the South end of Wargrave-read, in accordance with the Commission- ers instructiens, and reported that Mr. Pardey now stated that he. on Mr. Legh's behalf, disputed the necessity of the making of the road south of the chuPch gates, and will give no land for that purpose, neither would be pay any part of tlte expenses of the makinv of the road from that point. He also reported that Mr. Pardey had informed him that Mr. Legh would still give the land for the widening of the road no to the church gates. A long discussion ensued, when it was resolved that the making of the road south of the churrch gates be not proceeded with, and that the Law Clerk and Surveyor be instructed not to communicate with Mr. Pardey further upon the matter."—The Chairman re• marked that it seemed very bard if that piece of road should be left as it was at present. It seemed hard to him that the houses abutting upon the road and paying highway rates should have the road before them so that it was not fit to go along in winter time. It was a road which Was very much used.—Mr. Forster observed that part 0 the road was very bad indeed in winter. He could speak of it himself, as he often went along it —The Cehairman.said he thought if the Beard had power to have the road made good they ought to compel it to be done.—Mr. Glover said he took it that the Commissioners had power under the Act of Parliament to make the read good, and charge the owners of the property with the cost of the road, but Mr. Pardey, repre,enting the largest owner in the township was the person who said to the Board "If you make that road we shall not pay for It." They had power to make the road and charge the owner with it-, but rather than do that the Commissioners had thoughtlproper not•to take that course, but to allow the tenants of Mr. Legh, who, with ethers, would suffer by the state of the road, tc complain about the roads.—Mr. Forster askeeAf the Commissioners had not power to forcibly acquire possession of the road to a certain width.—The Chairman said the Commissioners had power to actiire the laud abutting on the road if they re- quired it to a certain width.—Mr. Gillespie said it seented to him that the Commissioners as a Board were a nonenity and perfectly useless if their decisions could he set aside, and that they must not do a single thing without the con- sent of an individual in, the place.—The Chairman remarked that he was just going to say that.—Mr. Hunt said the Board had power to do the work and charge the property owner with the work.—Mr. Gillespie: We have not done so owing to Mr. Pardey's objection. The thing has been allowed to stand over.—The Chairman did not think the Commissioners were taking a proper stand in the matter. Mr. Hunt said he thought the Commissioners ought to carry out the work. It was monstrous that people should suffer all through the winter and have to wade through water and mud.—Mr. Glover said he took that view himself, but, as they were in a difficulty with Mr. Ekrdey, they did not wish to clash in law with him. The resolution of the committee was simply moved in the hope that Mr. Pardey might change his views and meet the 13oard in a more favourable way.—The Chairman did not think the matter ought to ba allowed to drop without being further considered.—Mr. Emmett thought the best plan wonld be to let the matter rest where it was until the tenants of Mr. Legh made a com- plaint about the road.—The Chairman : I cannot get away from my house without getting up to my anees in mud.— Mt. Glover said all the people from the Vatican and E tries- town passing down the road sulered in the same waY.—The minutes were then passed_

APPALLINC- SUDDEN DEATH OF A TRADESMAN. Mr. Thomas Ellison, a highly respected and well-knowrr grocer and baker, carrying on businasa. at 242, Earle-street. Earlestown, died under circumstances of an extremely Pain" fut sudden nature en Wednesday forenoon. The deceased left home about ten o'clock in charge of a horse and bread-, Tan for the purpose of delivering bread to his customers- On his round he passed through Newton :thorny after eleven ;o'clock, and returned along Park-road and' past tee Cemetery to Wargrave. While driving along Park-road he met 3 woman named Alice Tra7is, who resides-in Regent-street, Earlestown. Mr.- Ellison assisted Mrs.-Trayis on her waY by asking her into his van. As they were rising along the road Mr. Ellison suddenly fell from his seat to the bottom of the van. He appeared to be in a fit, and, Mrs. Travis made an effort to restore cansciousnoss by rubbing his hands, &c. He al not recover, however, and Mrs. Travis at once drov6 to the Victoria Inn, Wargrave, where she intormed the landlady, Mrs. Harrison, of the sad aff dr. The two women got asaistance, and endeavoured to admit," ister brandy to the unconscious man, but they were unable to do so. At this time Mt. Ellison seemed tolie 02aite dead, and he was driven home.where Dr. Foulson was- called. That gentleman quickly attended, and pronounced life to be eN• tinct, probably from appoplexy. The deceased gentleman was well known throughout the district for his kind and genial disposition, and won the esteem of those with whern he was brought in contact. About twelve months ago the deceased had an appoplectic fit, and since then he has frequently complained of a pain in his side and stomach, as if suffering from indigestion. Dr. Patterson, of Earlestown, has attended him from that time up to his unfortunate death.
THE TOWNSHIP SEWERAGE SCHEME'. STA RTI 0 03 NM W WORKS.

The completion of at; ex;nsiv;-sch-e-in-e-for the disposal' of the sewage waste water of the Newton township was sig- nalised on Thursday afternoon, when the first trial of the machinery and works erected in a field at Rl/4d Bank, off Park-road, Newton, took place. Up to the present the sew- age of the greater portion of Earlerown and Newton hag been allowed to run along, a sort of of open drain, in the Mesnes, and thence into the stream known as Nswton Brook. In the district the stench, at times has been almost unbearable, and its effect upon the health of the neighborhood has not been a rery pleasant one. To do away with this disgraceful nuisance, the present works—including the erection of Hanson's automatic sewage machine were corn- mence.d about twelve months ago. 'Cho courge of the open drain across: the Mesnes was considerably diverted and covered in, and an outlet was formed a abort distance from the Newton Brook in a field adjoin- ing cemetery in Park-road.

The new scheme was formally tried on Thursday after- noon when among the gentlemen present were Mr. Hanson, the inventor, Mr. W. F. Gooch, .LP., chairman of the New - toe Improvement Commissioners, and Mr. Richard Brier- ley, clerk and surveyor. The scheme just completed in- cludes the reception of the sewage, and its thorough purification, prior to its discharge into the brook. The advantages of this—so far as the public health is concerned—are incalculable. The total works have necessitated the spending of about £l,OOO, mak' log a total expenditure of about zio,ooo, in connection with the township sewers. The extent of the works may be surmised from the fact that on an average about 150,000 gallons of sewage water rush along the drains, while the works are capable of dealing with about three times that quantity. The arrangements for dealing with the sewage appear to be of an extremely simple character. The sewage first enters what is known as the chemical or mixing house, and then passes through a course of three tanks, each about fifty feet in length and twenty feet wide, finally passing through a building called the " lever-house". into pipes whine convey what is almost pure water into the brook. The machinery is worked by the water Itself, thus saving all manual labour. One por- tion of the machinery in the chemical house, through which the sewage first enters, is fitted with bees made to move abcut and discharge the proper quantity of chemicals requirel to " treat " the sewage. The materials used in puri- fication of the sewage are lime and black ash w.ste, which cause all the solid particles of matter to fall to the bottom of one of the tanks. Immediately the lime and black ash waste fall into the sewage a series of revolving plates thor- oughly mix the ingredients, and a perfect system of purifi.. cation is carried out. The sewage next falls into the tanks, along which it slowly passes. In the first tank all the heavier particles fall to the bottom; the next tank re- ceives those a little lighter, while the lightest of all are de- posited in the third tank, and the water passes clear, bright, and free from impurities into the "lever-house." Here the motive power for the whole of the machinery is constructed. The water from the tanks falls into a pair of "levers," wedge shaped, and erected in the form of iron boxes. They each have a fall of about 24 inches, and are so made that when one is full of water the other is empty. The weight of the water causes the full box to de- scend and the empty one to ascend. At that moment the water in the full box is released and escapes, while a door in the empty box is closed and thus remains until the weight of the water forces it down. This machinery is connected with wire ropes to the machinery in the chemical house, and the rising and falling of the boxes is amply nal. • cient to keep the mixing apparatus in motion. In order to allow time for clearing out the deposits in the tanks, another set of three tanks running alongside those in use, have been built, and the liquid can be run into all or either of them without the slightest difficulty or convenience. It is stated that not only does Ilanson's pro- cess purify the sewage passing; through it, but the affluent water discharged Irons the machinery, actually purifies any surreptitious matter found in the river or stream into which it runs.

Prisoner was on Saturday behaving in a qiarrelsome manner in Tanners-lane, and, as he was drunk and disorderly, he was taken into custody. On the way to the police staticn Constable Bickley noticed that he was wearing a pair of new boots, and that r as boot had no lace in it. It was afterwards found that they had been stolen from the shop of Mr. Haynes. Prisoner, who said that be bought the boots, had been ten times previoasly before the magis- trates, and was now sent to prison for three months with bard labonr.

On Saturday evenine, Mr. Michael Roach Kelly, J.P., of Fargroye, county Clare, was fired at and wounded when on his way home from Ennis, after attending the Quarter Ses- sions. Six arrests have ben made. BOYCOTTING EXTRAORDINABY.—It is stated that rather than travel with an &rent of the Margeis of Ely's. who has evicted some tenants, 200 persons left a steamer at Water- ford on Saturday, and that the' Nationalists of Waterford" provided cars for their uee. At a Nationalist meeting at Longhrea, on Sunday, at which Messrs. Dillon, Redmond, and Sheehy, M.P.'s, were present, a disturbance aroma between the people and the police, the latter having to draw their swords and betons,and keep armed guard throughout the proceedings. The special correspondent of the " Irish Times" learns that strong representations have been made to the Govern- ment in favour of suppressing the Natioeal League, at least in disturbed districts. On the other hand, strong pressure has been brought to bear upon the Irish Government by landlords and others to prevent such a step. It is urged that the League is approaching its end, and will soon die of inanition, and that measures for its suppression would only stimulate its lagging spirits and supply its supporters with a grievance. It is believed that the policy of letting it severely alone will be adopted. Tree REIGN or TERROR IN IRELAND.—A striking case of boycotting is described in Saturday's "Irish Times," by a sufferer who signs himself "V." He says that having taken a farm in the open market he was banned. He has had 20 acres of produce rotting on the ground for several weeks, which nobody dare assist in saving, though he has offered 103 per day as wages. He cannot buy food, get horses shod, ac., at a less distance than 16 miles, though in his vicinity there are 45 public-houses, most of which sell provisions. He publishes is case in contradiction of Mr.l Justice Day's statement at the Belfast inquiry, that nobody was boycotted except landlords. A LONGSTANDING FEUD.—Early on Saturday, a shoot- ing affray occurred in Belfast, in which a man named Dev- lin nearly cost his life. It appears that Devlin was sitting on the window sill of his house, when two brothers, named Arthur and Thomas Lavery, poulterers, came up and began speaking to him. Suddenly, Thomas Lavery took a tevol- ver from his pocket, and fired three shots at Devlin, one lodging in his chest. The two brothers were immediately arrested. The injured man was conveyed to the Royal Hospital, where, in the presence of both prisoners, his de- position was taken. The affray is supposed to be the out- come of a longstanding feud. THE BELVAST ELECTION ,PRTITION.—At the sitting of the Court on Monday. Mr. Kisbey, for the petitioner, hav- ing intimated that counsel for the respondent agreed with him as to the correctness of the list of voters submitted at the commeecement of the trial. The Rev. M. Convey, presi- dent of the local branch of the National League, the first witness examined, denied that he had sent telegrams to militiamen at Devonport, offering to pay fhe expenses of their journey to Belfast, to enable them to vote. The petitioner's case having elosen, The McDermot. opened for the respondent. Having twitted the other side on not claim- ing the seat, he argued that there was not a tittle of evi- dence given to convince the Court that anything further had occurred than a few half-drunken men having, of their Own freewill, personated two or three voters. During coun- sel's address, a lengthy discussion ensued regarding the pe- titioner'a right to refer to marked registers of voters. On Wednesday, Baron Dowse and Mr. Justice O'Brien, in de- livering judgment, declared Mr. Sexton to have been duly elected, and that Mr. Haslett, the petitioner, should pay the cuss. After the decision there was some stone throwing in the direction of Crumlin-road, but no serious disturbance, rain helping to keep the streets clear, and the police disper- sing the disorderly crowd which had assembled. PIGS.

CRUELTY TO -.J.-At Wrexham Police Court, on Monday, Matthew Lowe, pig deiler, St. Helens, waq tined 12s Cu, including costs, for ill-treating a number of pigs by putting too many into a float for conveyance from Wrex- ham Smithfield to the railway stAtion.

FIRE IN A GLASSWORE.S.—On Thursday a fire was discovered in the old gashouse at Ravenhead Glassworks. A number of men at once poured wtter from buckets upon the flames, which were soon extinguished. A large wooden screentwas burned away and the roof damaged. About £l5 damage was done, and that is covered by insurance in the Norwich office. TIIE FAILURE OF EX•ALDEIIMAN E. JOIINSON. - At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Mr. John_ son, an ex-Mayor of St. Helens, and a groce.r and provision dealer, having shops in that and several of the surrounding towns, appeared for his adjourned public examination. Questions were put to him as to the reason why certain ac- counts relating to furniture bad been put into the name of his wife when formerly they were in his own. The debtor denied having p suggested the alterations, or even knowing ef them until that day. It was, however, perfectly true that such accounts were paid by his wife out of her own income, and she kept a small memorandum book, in which her in- come and expenditure were entered. The Registrar said ha would require to peruse the evidence Mrs Johnson had given on the matter, and adjourned the examination for a fortnight.

Mr. Thornton also added, witness alleged, that he (Payne) and others,ought to havoi)een riding in their carriages at that time.—Defendants were also ex- amined, and swore that Mr. Thornton had admitted that he had papers in his possession which would entitle the art family to the property.—A Mrs. Hart alleged that Mr. Thornton took her mother-im- law's will, which left all the property to the Hart family, off a chest of drawers at her mother-in-law'a house ten ortisrelve years ago. She had asked for its return on several occasions.—Mr. Stubs said the ' magistrates Iltml considered the question very care- fully. The d4)fendants had done., what was in the opinion of the Bench., nn impro- per thing in going to a man's house in such numbers; and in an apparently uproarious manner, implying threats, if not actually using them. They were, however, just outside the law, and the magistrates would give them the benefit of the doubt and dismiss the summonses. The magis- trates cautioned the defendants about their future conduct.—Mr. Thornton then handed to defendants a. will, which it was, said was the only document in reference to the matter that he had, and the defen- dants promised not to repeat the conduct for -which they had been summmed.

Whilst potatoes falled in those years,. the wheat, cats, and barley crops were never known to be more productive, and there were numerous herds of c;›,,Ale and flocks of sheep that would have provided splendid food for the serving people. But to prov:de the revenue of Cee absentee landlords 11 millions of people wee,e allowed to die of starvation in sight of the prod Mt of farmls that their own labour had helped to producer (Shaine.) The dead bodies were huddled shroudless into arcotlinless grave like the rotten carcases of animals rather than the British Givernment would tax the absentee landlords for the price of a..%vr deal boards to cover the deao bodies of Ithe starving thousands of mankind. (Shame.) This was one result of the Act of Union. The efforts to effect reforms 5n the land laws—reforms that would pernat the tenant to share in the produce of his own industry, and whicie would have compelled the landlord to return a portion of the rent which be had exacted from the people—all efforts at reform wore met by Government, Liberal and Tory alike, with the most contemptcumand most practical refusal and rejections. They knew how lung it took the British Uoexern- ment to pass the Act of Catholic elnsncips6on. The people passed through 29 years of hope- less coercion and the vilest tyranny before they were releeesed from the burden of penal enactments. At that thee 70 and 80 per cent, of the British army was composed e Irish Catholic soldiers, wad in defence of the empire were shedding their blood upon the battle fields of Spain, Bel- gium,and France. Even those Irish soldiers who died upon the fields of Spain and. Belgium were denied the reward in their last moments of the consolation of a priest. They could eearch the history of mankind through, and ingrati- tude like this t CT would not find. (Applause.) Since the Act of 'Jnion, through the neglect of the British Govern- ment the homesteade of Ireland bad been broken up, her people were scattered over all the face of the habitable globe, her-flourishing manufactures had declined, and they were a monument of the injustice done to Ireland. (Ap- plause.) The state of tbe country called out for a remedy. The restoration of that Parliament of which they were. so unjustly deprived was imperatively demanded if they were once more to experience the prosperity, the happiness, and the wealth that Ireland knew when she had her own Parliament in 1782. (Ap- plause.) The Irish Nationalists by their organisation had compelled one British party-to make the settlement of the Irish question a main plants in their platform, and they had happily as their leader, the greatest statesman of the age in I.the person of Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) From their trQ combined exertions the day could not be far distant when they would reverse the state of things that now obtained.' This was the nroverbial darkk hour that preceded the dawn, and already the man who was skilled in political foresight =lid see signs upon the horizon of approaching victory, and the cause of Home Rule for Lreland was assured. (Ap- plause.)_
