div.head: TRAGIC ATTEMPTED SUICIDE
div.p: THE TRAGIC ATTEMPTED SUICIDE

AT E A.RLESTOWN. Oa Saturday afternoon James McKenzie (46), des- cribed as a ship's engineer, of Liverpool, was corn- witted for trial by the Newten-le-Willows justices, at their Petty Sessional meeting in the Town Hall, for attenspting to take away hie life, on the 14th ult., at Eerlestown, by shooting himself with a revolver. Mr. Stewart defended the prisoner, whose appearance was emaciated. Considerable interest was evinced in the proceedings, the affair having caused no little excite- tnent in the neighbourhood. The eircumeteneee of the nice were narrated to the magistrates by Police-Supt. Weir. They are so well known KS to require but brief recapitulation. On the afternoon of the four- teenth of last month prisoner went to Earlestown to see his wife, from whom he had been separated. The door was fastened, and he knocked several times. No notice, hewever, was taken. Prisoner then sat down en the step. and, pulling a revolver from his rocket, fired and shot himself under the right ear. 11-e then placed the weapon at his side, and became unconecione. Dr. Paterson, of Eerlestown, who was in the neigh- bourhood, exaelined the injured man, and by his in- struetions McKenzie was removed to the Royal Infir- mary at Liverpool. Four of the chambers of the re- volver were after wards found to contain ball cartridges, and the other two chambers were empty. One an- peered to have been recently fired. Prisoner remained some days in the infirmary, and on being discharged he was apprehended and taken in custody to Newton, Iwhere, on the following Monday, he was brought be- fore the magistrates, charged with the offence, and remanded to the Petty Sessions. Prisoner was a widower with four children when he married his present wife, who, some time ego, in consequence of domestic differences, returned to Earle-street, Earlestown, to live with Mrs. Mottram, her mother. Evidence was given by Mrs. Mottram, who said that prisoner was her son-in-law—to her sorrow. He married her daughter about two Tears ago, but she left him about ten months since. On several occasions during the past ten months she had seen him at her house in Eerlestown, and had sometimes admitted him. Lat- terly she had been afraid of him, and had therefore refused to let him enter the house. On the day in question witness, hearing that he was coming, locked the door. He tapped lightly and then tried to look through the window. Not receiving a reply, he knocked loudly, and witness directly afterwards heard the report of a pistol. On looking through the window she saw her son-in-law sitting on the door- step. Blood was flowing freely from a wound in his neck. In answer to questions put to her by Mr. Stewart, witness said that prisoner was addicted to drink, but had other bad habits in addition. He and ' bis wife lived happily together for a time, when he was sober.—Evidence was next given by a girl named Sarah Evans, who said that as she was passing through Earle•street she saw prisoner pull the pistol produced from his pocket and shoot himself somewhere under the right ear.—Medical testimony was adduced by Dr. Paterson to the effect that he was driving along Earle-streei; on the day in question when his atten- tion was called to the prisoner, who was bleeding from a wound in the neck, underneath the right ear Witness staunched the wound and ordered his removal to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. At that time he did not think the man would live, as he considered the wound to be a very dangerous one. On being searched by P.C. Hughes. twelve ball cart- ridges were found in prisoner's possession. On behalf of prisoner Mr. Stewart said that unfortunately his client had given way to intemperate habits, which had brought him to his present position. When he first married his second wife he lived happily with her, and it was only when he gave way to drink that his wife declined to live with him. No allega- tion was made against him that he went to Earles- town with any intention of doing violence to himself. He simply went to see hie wife and chili, with the hope that he might induce his wife io live with him again For a fortnight before he had been drinking ,hard, and was in a mad state of intoxication when he got to the house. On being refused admittance he committed the rash act, but he had no intention to destroy his life. Tie was a respectable man and the lesson he had received, Mr. Stewart trusted, would be a warning to him. His offence had been fully ex- piated by his imprisonment since his recovery, and by the remorse he felt at what he had done. He asked the magistrates to be lenient as prisoner had four children d-pendent on him. The magistrates intimated that the case was of so serious a character that they had no option but to commit the prisoner for trial.

The prisoner was brought up at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Wednesday, and Mr. Vrelsby, barrister, prosecuted. After the facts of tiae case had been stated, the Chairman said the prisoner did not appear to have attempted to injure anybody but him self.—The prisoner, who had been kept in custody since his apprehension, was ordered to be discharged at the rising of the Court.

A DISPUTED WILL AT WARRINGTON.' At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, John Hart, Thomas Hart, Richard Baxter, Ann Salt, Ellen Payne, and Mary Hart were sum- moned for being unlawfully on the premises of Henry Thornton, at Fearnhead, on the 23rd ult., and conducting themselves in a noisy, disorderly, and turbulent manner, to his annoyance. Mr. Percy ' Davies appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Wal- ton, barrister, Liverpool, defended.—Mr. Davies said that Mr. Thornton was an agent, and resides at the , Laurels, Fearnhead Cross, Fearnhead. Some years ago he transacted a little business for the defen- dants in endeavouring to get them some property which they were under the impression they were ' entitled to. He thought it was only fair to mention that that was the bone of con- tention. The defendants had been to his (Mr. Davies') office, and were under the impression that they were the rightful owners of some pro- perty possessed by Mrs Triphena Tunstall. It ap- peared that many years ago there was a lady who was known in Warrington as "Lady Hart," and the defendants claimed that they were descendants of that lady. Some 60 years ago "Lady Hart " left a will which was proved at Chester, and her property was left to the Tanstalls. Mr. Davies had told de- fendants that it was no use wasting their money in proceeding with the matter, and they were also re- commended to get the advice of counsel, who gave them a similar opinion. Mr. Thornton's name crop- ped up in Connection with the matter, and the de- fendants charged him with having in his possession certain documents, which ought, it was alleged, to have been delivered up, and which would have entitled them to the property. Mr. Thorn- ton denied this, and on Saturday, the 23rd ultimo, the whole of the defendants, who lived in Warrington, went to his house about four o'clock in the afternoon, and said they wanted to see Mr. Thornton, and that they would have him out of the house. They made a great noise, and Mr. Thornton was afraid to go out, thinking discretion the better part of valour, and he gave an order for a policeman to be sent for, as the defendants con- tinued their noisy conduct for about an hour. No one on the premises dared to go out. Mr. Davies submitted that the behaviour of the defendants ought not to be allowed, and if their worships thought it was a proper case to have brought be- fore the Court, he should ask them to bind the de- fendants over to keep the peace.—Mr. Thornton gave evidence showing that the defendants went to his house on the day named, and cursed and swore loudly. He was afraid of the whole of the defendants, and although they asked him to come out of the house he thought it advisable to remain inside. Defendants had annoyed him in the streets on several occasions.—ln cross-examination, witness stated that he had drawn out the will of William Hart, and had it in his possession. Ho had not told anyone that he had papers in his possession which would entitle the defendants to the property. Defendants did not ask for the will; but on every occasion they asked for papers which they alleged lie had in his possession.—Mr. Walton submitted that there was no case made out, and that the de- fendants could. not be bound over to keep the peace, as no threats were used, and the complainant did not go in any bodily fear. Mr. Thornton had brought this annoyance on himself by stating that he had got something in his possession which would en- title the defendants to the property, and which he refused to show them. He (Mr. Walton) did not deny that the defendants went to Mr. Thornton's house, and that they shouted to him to give up cer- tain papers.—For the defence he called John Broad- hurst, of Pinner's-brow, who said he remembered seeing Mr. Thornton and Mrs. Payne on the Bth of June this year. Mrs. Payne asked Mr. Thornton whether he had got any property belonging to "Lady Hart." He admitted that he had, and told her that she could not have the papers relating to it without he was paid for tlr.m. Samuel Payne, husband of one of the defendants, deposed that Mr. Thornton had told him that there was a lot of property that belonged to the Harts, and that he had papers and documents in his pos- session by which they could recover it. He also stated that Mrs. Triphena Tunstall had received the rents from the property since the death of "Lady Hart." Witness told Mr. Thornton that the rents must have amounted to a great deal, and the , latter told witness that the Hart family !

div.head: LECTURE ON IRELAND AT PZNCORN.
div.p: LECTURE ON IRELAND AT PZNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn branch of the Irish National League, a lecture was deliverer). in Bethesda Schoolroom on Wednesday evening by 3lr. D. J. Sweeney, the orga-aiser of the League for Lan- cashire district. There Ririe a good attendance. Dr. O'Keeffe, of Widnes, presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mess.rs. Moore, 0. Farrell, E: T. Williamson, J. Curzans, P. Whelan, T. Byrne, T. Finegan, and John Tooghau. The Criaiumax, in opening the proceedings, said the Uiaion" so called was carried in a most iniquitous manner, and it effects liad-heen calamitous and horrible.. Mr. Gladstone had hrought the question of Home Rule for Ireland before the House of Commons and the country in a manner with which they must all agree—(applause)—and undoubtedly it was a question that was becoming of greater Importance to the Enalish people. It did not now matter whether Itlr. liladatone was the Prime Minister or whether Lord Randolph Churchill—(groans)—held that position, the question of Home Rule was bound to be dealt with—(bear, hear)—and his advice to all friends of the cause was to iniuence all their fellows to vote for a member of Parliament who was, in favour of the regenera- tion of Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. E. Hul proposed a resolntien heattily congratulat- ing Mr. Sexton on his SOCCets in Belfast. (Applause.) After the national victories in Ulster, Mr. Bill thought they could claim to be the loyal party—(applause)—and all they wanted as loyalists was nothing more nor less than eqaal laws. (Applause.) He advised the voters to vote for Mr. Brunner at the next epoorthnity. He was a good man and true. (Applause.) Mr. T. Witaasassuar said the attempt to destroy national- istn in Belfast had failed ; their Cause had triumphed ; and he had much pleasure in seconding the resolution. The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. SWEENEY then delivered his lecture entitled " The union : its effects and remedy." His plea- sure at being amongst them that evening was enhanced by the fact that he found in the chair an old Irishman who had certainly seen many years' oervice in the Irish National cause. (Applause.) Long before he (the speaker) had the slightest idea that Ireland was in any manner unfairly dealt with Dr. O'Keeille had served a very honourable apprentice- ship in the Nationalist ranks. (Applause.) Before 1800, which was the date of the passage of the Act of Union by which the Irish Parliament was extinguished and united with that of England and Scotland at Westminster, Ireland bad complete power over all Irish affairs. During a couple of years preceding 1782 a great agitation was set afoot in Ireland for the purpose of putting an end to the interference of the Parliament of Greateßritaiu in the affairs of Ireland. Hitherto the Irish Parliament had to subject itself on almost every important occasion to the interference of either the British Cabinet or English courts of justice, not only with regard to law and, legislation, but even in matters of trade and commerce, to such an extent that Irish trade and commerce were crippled for the advan- tage of the British manufacturer and the British commercial man. (Hear, hear.) These things struck very deeply into the minds of Irish patriots, and Flood and Grattan fomented an agitation with a great and powerful eloquence that touched the pride of the people. The Irish gentry enrolled an army of a hundred thousand volunteers, and the British Parliament was compelled to pees an Act in which it was recited that there was no power but King, Lords, and Com- mons of Ireland that had any right to legislate for people of Ireland. This Act formed the basis and constitution of what was known as Grattan' a Parliament Under that Par- liament Ireland prospered greatly; and it was a strange thing that this Grattan's Parliament, of which they spoke with such affection and pride, was not representative if the whole Irish people. In that Parliament Catholics had no right to sit, and further no Catholic could vote for any member to sit in that house. From 1712 to 1800 religious toleration was not very plentiful is this island; bigotry held mighty sway over the people of Great Britain, yet this Irish Parliament. Protestant though every one of its members was, in 1783 passed an Act, which swept away five-sixths of the penal code that had been, passed by the Irish and Eng- lish Parliaments to crush the Irish Catholics during the previous two centuries. (Applause.) Bat they were proud • of this parliament for a more material reason. In the short time that it existed their little island made as much pro- gress in manufacturing and commercial wealth, as any other country in the whole globe was known to progress at the time. (Applause.). he Irish Parliament had not a very large amount of money to pay for the government of the country. It had not to support very large military estab- lishments for the purpose of compelling people to abide its behests, and as a conseqpenee it imposed very slight taxes upon the people, but no matter how slight the taxes the Chancellor of the Exchecater was able to report a great balance in favour of the nation, and with a patriotism that had not been excelled by any Parliament of the time, the Irish Government from time to time disposed of large sums of money yearly in bounties to promote the industries and manufactures of the country. Thousands of Irish families were supported by the manufacturing industry fostered by the national Parlia- ment, and people were not then obliged to leave their native land starving and in tattered garments for the purpose of finding a livelihood in strange lands in every part of the globe. (Applause.) During the years he had mentioned the consumption of tea and coffee and wine,which furnished a very fair indication of the condition of the people, in- creased at the rate of 180 per cent. While in England and other countries the consumption did not increase one tenth of the rate. This progress of Ireland in manufacturing and commercial wealth excited the jealousy of the English man- ufacturers and commercial =en ; hence they resolved to destroy the Matt Parliament to incorporate Ireland with Great Britain in one Parliament, and in that way to shunt aside the obstacle which opposed the pro- greats of England and Scotlarld. The Act of Union, so called, was then brought about by the most diabolical methode, which no less a person than Mr. Gladstone had denounced in the strongest language. The Government of Pitt dis- tributed in bribes to the Protestant members of the Irish Parliament no less a sum than millions which at that time was a very large sum indeed ; whilst, still further to corrupt the members, titles—marquisates, earldoms, baronet- ciee, and positions in the army were conferred galore. The country was failed with troops, and nobody dared to open his mouth in denunciation of the per- fidy of the ministers and hirelings in Ireland, for if he did so be was immediately cast into prison. The Irish Catholics were told that the first act of the Unien Parliament would be to emancipate them com- pletely and admit them to all rights, political and religious, which their Protestant fellow countrymen enjoyed. By these various means the Act of Union was passed ; but when the fatal day arrived there were 120 faithful Protestant members of the Irish Parliament who by their opposition to the measure proved their incorruptibility and their refusal to barter away the rights of the Irish nation. (Applause.) The lecturer contended and quoted historical anthorities to show that the Irish people never acquiesced in the Union, and described that the first effect was that all the landed gentry of Ireland the moment the Irish Parliament ceased to sit gave up their establishments in Dublin and throughout Ireland and established themselves in London. From that time dated the vile system of absenteeism through which Ire- land had lost an annual sum of £5,000,000 of money. It would not be at all unjust to say that since the Act of Union Ireland had lost by the absence of the landed gentry upwards of 430 millions of money. One of the most usual objections made to agitation in Ireland was that it preven- ted the influx of British capital into that country. "Only be quiet," said the Tories, "and you will see how British capital will flow into your country, and how your manufac- tures will progress." Ireland had had periods of quiet when there was no sound to be heard save the groan of dis- tress or the cry of want—nothing to interfere with the lux- urious happiness of the British ministers and the British people. Then there was not the slightest flow of British capital into the country. The quieter they were the more the landlords fleeced them arm robbed them. (Ap- plause.) What they wanted was that they would leave their own Irish capital in the country, , and net give power to the army, navy, and police force in Ireland to assist British and Irish landlords resident out of Ireland to continue to fleece and rob the people to the extent they had been rob- bed for the last century. (Applause.) As a result of ab- senteeism the Irish tenant farmers found every day it was increasingly laborious to live upon the land. After bringing bog and morass into a state of fertility they had found the produce of their labour confiscated by the landlord who lived in the lap of luxury in London whilst the tenants were toiling from morning till night, and obliged to subsist upon a few meals of potatoes or Indian corn and their chil- dren compelled to go about without even clothing to cover their nakedness from the passing strangers. From 1800 to the present time, for the purpose of making the Irish people swallow the British pill of absentee landlordism there had passed the House of Commons 80 Coercion Acts. Besides, through this absenteeism, and through tha neglect of the B:itish Government, there had been three very severe famines in Ireland, especially the one in 1840-47-43. Statis.

div.p: EARLE STO WN.

WITHOUT A TICZET.—At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on WeJsesday. Walter Roebuck, of Liver- pool, was charged with travelling without ticket from Liverpool to Newton Bridge on in-sday. The prisoner arrived by the 4-0 express from Lime-street and handed to Ticket-collector Harron an exhibition excursion ticket, the date on which it was found, had been altered with lead pencil. The prisoner refused, to pay the fare demanded, and he was given into custody. The prisoner was fined 5s and costs.

ALLEG3D WIFJ3 ASSAULT AT MeLLESTOIV.Z.T. herb Naylor, of Earlestown, appeared against her husband, Marcus Naylor, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, and complained to the magistrates that he assaulted her son the 10th of last month. she• slated that on the even- ing of that day he abused her, was very violent, knocked her down, and kicked and struck her several times. The husband then gave his version of the alair. He alleged that his wife, instead of attending to her ditties, was at the house of her mother, and that because he told her that he had not married the w kola of the family she struck him. He thought, he said, that it was time he should "do some- thing," and alleged that his wife had in various wave neg- lected him. She had deceived Hui about money matters, in consequenca of which he had been thrown out of a club, and had taken the bed aad other things, reducing him to the necessity of sleeDing on a mattrass with an overcoat and a jacket for covering. She bad left him of her ewn accord. The magistrates die miseed the case. EABLESTOWN PRIAKTITI METUODLsT MUTUAL IN. PROWECANT bOCIETY.—This society held its inaugural meeting on Tnes,av evening, when the chair was occupied kry Mr. Thomas Clark, vice-president. He said he believed the society would be a great boon to the members iradivi- dually„providing it was their objpct to get good. He asked all present to do their best to make it mentally, morally, and religiously successful:—Mr. .1. Hollycock said they ' needed, as members of a,Christian church, all the knowledge and improvement they could get in this age of progress, and be believed the class would ba a great source of benetit to those who wished to avail themselves of its privileges.—Mr. J. Woods pointed out the advisability of getting as many of the Sunday school senior scholars into the class as passible. He felt sure it would be a great benefit to them, and hoped all present would do what they could to induce the scholars to attend. A general dissuasion ensued, in which Messrs. J. Pearce, T. Traverse, W. Pearson, J. Jackson, and others took Dart. The meeting was brought to a close by singing the Doxology.

&LOC-MEC-) AOC-MEET AT P.Ant-P.s.roWzr. William Saul, a young man, employed as a moulder's apprentice at the engineering works of, Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, Earles- town. mat with a sad accident on Tuesday morning, by which he sustained injpries of a serious chiracter. The un- fortunate man was engaged working on his knees at a mould in one of the boxes, almost under a machine known as "the traveller," used for the purpose of conveying moulding boxes, &c., from one position to another. While Saul was so engaged, the "traveller" was being used by another employe of the firm. Without any warning, and from some unexplained cause, a. large wheel connected with the " tra- Teller " gave way, and it fell from overhead, alighting heavily on Sault. The wheel weighed about 2cwt., and in its descent it struck Saul, on the head and shoulder, the key of the wheel causing a fearful gash on the left side of the his head, laying bare the skull. The wheel also crashed upon Saul's leg, causing a deep lacerated wound, and other- wise bruising his body. Several men at once ran towards Saul, and he was removed to his home, where Dr. Foulson saw him immediately afterwards. The injured man was quite unconscious, and was found to be in a very precarious condition. Up to Thunsday afternoon Saul was still alive, but he was far from being out of danger. The painful acci- dent occasioned great sympathy throughout the town. Saul was one of the playing members of the 2nd team' of the Earlestown Football. Club, and his absence will be felt in the ranks of the players.. THE CHARGE OR Eliza PRETENCES AGAINST TRADES- MAN.—At the Liverpool Quarter Stssions, on Wednesday, the charge against Thomas Bell, picture frame maker and gilder, Earlestown, of haying, on the 22nd September, ob- tained by false pretences, from Thomas Abraham Pimble, jeweller, &c., a gold albert chain, value .£5, Came on for hearing. Mr. Robert Pierpoiat, of Warrington, prosecuted, and Mr. Cottingham,. barrister, instructed by Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, defended. The charge was altered to 43119 of feloniously stealing the guard, and the evidence given at the formal hearing at Newton and previously reported ssas re- peated. The only additioual witness was Mrs. Pimblett, mother of the prosecutor, who deposed that au hour after the prisoner bad obtained the guard she went to the priso- ner's house and asked for the chain', b it the prisoner refused to give it up.—For the defence Mr. Cottinghain contended that the prisoner had obtained the guard on certain condi- tions, and that he had not had the opportunity to fulfil those conditions. He pointed out that the prisoner had been committed for trial on a charge of false pre- tences, but at the sessions he had been indicted for larceny, , and the prosecution knew that the first charge could not be sustained. He submitted therefore there was no case to go to the jury.—The Chairman (the Earl of Derby) in addres• sing the jury, said he thought the prisoner had given a true account of the affair in saving to the police officer that it was a "drunken spree." There did not appear to be any evidence to show that the prisoner did not intend to pay for the chain honestly, though he did a foolish thing in pawn- ing it.—The jury returned a verdict of "Not guilty," and the prisoner was discharged. CO-OPERATITE BoCIETY CONCERT.—The first of a series of concerts under the auspices of the Earlestown In- dustrial Co-operative Society was given in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Saturday night. For the occasion some of the most popular of local artistes kindly gave their services. There were was a very large attendance. The concert commenced with the song, "Over the rolling sea," finely rendered by Mr. P. Hastie, and Miss Owen following with a nicely sung piece," Fairly caught." Mr. A. Holds- worth (clarionette) and Mr. A. Caldwell (pianoforte) were warmly encored for a musical duet ; after which MT. S. Swann was recalled for his clever rendering of "Heroes." He gave, in response, "Trusty as steel." The popular humourist, Mr. J. Williams, gave "The little nigger," and in response to the encore gave "The show-man."; Messrs. E.. Corlett and W. Turner fairly well sung the duet, "The tented field," and the last named also gave "Tom Bowling." "Under the Old Flag" was effectively given by Mr. S. Swann, who was again recalled. His second item was "Our Jack's come home to-day." Mr. J. Har- rison was successful in his comic selection, en- titled "The Irish christening," and on receiving an en- core gave "The darkie's courtship." "Banbury Cross" was sung by Miss Owen, and Mr. Hastie appeared to great advantage in "Afloat on the ocean." He was deservedly re- called, whereupon he gave "The white squall." He was followed by Mr. J. Williams, who created prolonged enthu- siasm by his "banjo eccentricity." and Miss Owen and Mr. Turner were applauded for their rendering of the duet " The soldier's farewell.,' The entertainment then closed with a laughable farce entitled "Shaving done here," the characters in which were capitally represented by Messrs. P. Hastie, J. Williams, John Jones, John Bailey, Joseph Harrison, and T. Singleton, Mr. A. Caldwell ably aCenme paled the vocal selections on the pianoforte,

An American editor vents his rage as follows :—" We would say to the rascal who stole our shirt off the pole while we lay in bed waiting for it to dry, that we sin- cerely hope that the collar may cut his throat." WORKING-MEN'S INFIRMARY CONCERT. On Saturday evening the annual entertainment prOmoted by the Warrington Infirmary Working- men's Committee was held in the Public Hall, the Mayor presiding. Hitherto the entertainment has been of the nature of a miscellaneous concert, the programme being carried out by local performers, assisted by some professional talent, te..t this year the committee sought variety, and engaged Mr. Mac Hale, who has won considerable reputation by his clever performances, to give his monologue entertainment. There was a large attendance, though rather less than on some previous occasions. It should be mentioned that all the arrangements were gratuitously carried out by members' of the Working-men's Committee. The MA.YOR, in the course of a short introductory address, mentioned that he had received an apology for being ' unable to attend from Alderman Davies who haa always taken a warm interest in the Infirmary. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the work of the corn- ' inittee, the Mayor said that formerly the contribu- tions to the Infirmary from the works in the town rarely exceeded £5O a year, but on the first year after the committee taking the matter in hand, that was 1880, the amount rose to £165 Os 31d. (Applause.) In 1881 the amount obtained was £339 8s 10d; in 1882, .£363 5s 11. d; in 1883, £422 is 6d; in 1884, £397 19s 3d; and in 1885 the contributions amounted to the handsome sum of £47813s id. (Applause.) Ile thought these results were very creditable to the committee. (gear, hear, and applause.) The entertainment was h begun with a pianoforte solo by Mr. J. Batch- etldeenr, after which a variety of impersonations were given by Mr. Mac Hale. Amongst the most amusing were those of Mr. Ebenezer Blifkine, "a respectable old party, and distinguished father of a numerous family of spinsters," and Miss Angelina Blifkins, one of the said spinsters. "Evening party" absurdities gave Mr. Mac Hale an opening for some amusing strokes, as did also the characters of the " broken- . hearted" Frenchman, the Spanish troubadour, and the German bandsmen, the latter being described as a " realistic nuisance of the present," and the Spaniard a "romantic emblem of the past." Police- man xi. Susan Jane, Happy Dick, "a Lancashire lad fro' Bowton," and Barney O'Toole, a very "rare specimen of the old Irish piper," were all sources of amusement to the audience. The entertainment concluded with the "musical and mysterious naelo- drama." "The Pirate foiled; or the cruise of the Sarah Jane," and as Mr. Mac Hale represented the pirate and every other individual concerned in the very mysterious melodrama, he was given many opportunities of displaying the remarkable rapidity of his making a change of costume. The accom- paniments to the songs were throughout played by Mr. Batchelder.

Thomas, Mr. Francis Lawrinson, of Widnes, who has grocery and but- cher's establishments at Warrington, Widnes, Northwich Itancorn, &c., was charged with having, on the 15th October, exposed for sale in his shop, High-street, Runcorn, two pieces of beef unfit for the food of Dian. He was further charged with having, on the same premises, 15 pieces of beef and five pieces of mutton intended for sale, which were unfit for the food of man. Mr. W. 11. Linaker prosecuted for the Board of Commissioners, and Mr. T. J. Peters defended. The defendant pleaded not guilty to both charges. Mr. Linaker asked the magistrates if he satisfied them that Mr. Lawrinson was guilty to mark their sense of the conviction by imposing a substantial penalty. It was very wrong to come into 3 place like Runcorn and dispose of putrid food to the poor people. The defendant had rendered himself liable to a penalty of I;44o.—James Percival, inspector of nuisances, stated that on the 15th October from inforthation received he went to Mr. Lawrinson's for a piece of corned beef. The piece was putrid. He then went to the shop, and in the yard he was shown a cask, which contained about 24-cwt. of meat. At his request the manager brought a dish from the counter containing four pieces of beef. He took two of these pieces to the medical officer, who condemned them as unfit for food. In the cask were 68 pieces, 22 of which he , seized as bad. All the pieces he seized were destroyed by order of Mr. Brundrit, J.P.—By Mr. Peters :It was salt meat. About 12 months ago he had a dispute with Mr. Lawrinson, and sent him a letter, but.did not pursue the matter further. He took about 1501bs of beef.--Dr. McDougall, the medical officer of health, deposed to examining the meat. Part of the meat in the cask was good. All the pieces seized were in a putrid condition. The inspector had only done his duty in this case; and if he had not taken the action he did he (the doctor) would have reported him to his employers.—Mr. Peters took a preliminarY objection on the ground that the evidence did not show that Mr. Lawrinson had a guilty knowledge of the condition of the meat, but after some discussion he was over-ruled by the Bench. He then remarked that his client was a most respectable man, and would not on any ac- count allow a piece of putrid meat to be sold. There

AGGRAVATED ASAULT ON A WOMAN. At Warrington Borough Court. on Monday morn- ing, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and other magistrates, John Welsby, foreman fustian cutter, was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to Catherine Bate, wife of a forge labourer. who lives at 75, Stamford-street, on the evening of the 23rd of October. Subsequently the charge was reduced to one of aggravated assault. —Mr. Whittle (deputy town clerk), who prosecuted on behalf of the police, said that prisoner was the brother of James Welsby, landlord of the Golden Ball, who ' also had a fustian cutting shop at which he em- ployed prisoner as foreman. On the night in ques- tion the husband of the prosecutrix was in the public-house with a friend, and pro- secutrix went there for him. She heard him quarrelling with a man Lamed llamblett and told him to come away. High words passed, and prosecutrix pushed her husband out of the house. As she was doing so, it was alleged, pri- soner kicked her, inflicting a serious injury.—Evi- deuce was called to bear out the case for the prose- cution, and Dr. Adams described the injury received by Mrs. Bate, who, he said, was now out of danger —For the defence Mr. Jenkins urged that Welsby was not the man who inflicted the kick. He called several witnesses, who bore out the defence, and very contradictory evidence was given. In giving the decision of the Bench, the Mayor said that the magistrates were all of the opinion that the case was a gross one. They were convinced that prisoner inflicted the injury, and they wholly discredited almost every word of the evidence given for the defence He never heard such wholesale perjury in his life, and he believed that there was more than one witness who deserved to be committed for trial for perjury, the last one particularly so. It was established beyond all doubt that that man in particular c )mmitted perjury. Prisoner might thank his stars that he had not to take his trial for murder. He would be sent to prison for two months, and on his release would be called upon to find two sureties for his good behaviour for the six months then ensuing. He would also have to pay £2 15s Gd the costs. The Mayor added that it was only fair to say that Mr. Jenkins had acted with perfect propriety in the matter, and had done everything that a professional gentleman could do. Mr. Jenkins replied that his wish always was to elicit truth. On the conclusion of the business of the Court, the Mayor addressed John Cairns, one of the witnesses for the defence, who had been told not to leave the Court, and asked him what he meant by committing deliberate perjury, to which he replied that he had spoken the truth. The Mayor reiterated that Cairns had said what was utterly unreliable, and had been telling a pack of untruths. Chief Constable Hunt observed that Cairns deserved prosecution, and intimated that he should keep him in custody for an hour until he thought the matter over.—At the Borough Court, on Tuesday, two women named Letitia Ellis and Catherine Daley, who gave evidence on behalf of the prosecution on the day previous, attended before the magistrates.—Chief Constable Hunt explained that on Monday a serious charge of kicking was tried, and the women gave evidence. The prisoner, John Welsby, was foreman over the fustian cutting shop in which the two witnesses were employed, which belonged to Ins brother, James Welsby: After the trial they were discharged from their work, and he wished the Bench to order that they should be allowed something for having attended the court in connec- tion with the case on two occasions. They were thrown out of work at a moment's notice because they spoke thetruth, although they were summoned witnesses and came with reluctance. The Bench recommended that 3s be allowed to each.

PROPOSED GYMNASIUM FOR WIDNES. Sir.—l have been asked to endeavour to establish a gym- nasium at Widnes. I now beg to say that lam ready on any part to establish a branck of the National Physical Recreation Society, and if a suitable room can be obtained, will tit it up with the necessary apparatus and provide a teacher twice a week, providing I get sufficient encourage- ment from the young men of the town. I shall therefore be glad to receive names and addresses from intending mem- bers, and when a sufficient number is obtained, I will call a meeting to arrange details.—Your obedient servant, A. ALEXANDER. Liverpool Gymnasium, Nov. 4th, 1886.

EDUCATE! EDUCATE! EDUCATE! Sir,—Ou the fall of Mr. Gladstone's Government it was pretty generally admitted that the more fully the Irish ques- tion became understood by the constituencies, proportion- ately would opposition to Home Rule diminish; and we have the advice of Mr. Gladstone himself to study Irish history as a means to that end. It is need'ess to point to the one subject which will absorb and overshadow all others on the re-assembling of Parliament in a few months' time, and impossible is it to say how soon the whirligig of events may bring about disruption in the ranks of that combination whose first and boasted object is the exclusion from power of our " grand old chief " for the remainder of his days. sir, in face of these propositions, what educatioodl movement is it intended to set a-foot to give light to those amoug us (and I believe there are many) who are in doubt and darkness on this Irish question, and who I believe would gladly be instructed. What quickening influence is to be infused into our organisation in the shape of seed sowing and other preparations, without which there can he no harvest (except for other than Liberal bands to gather). Are we to continue with folded hands, blinking and sleep- ing whilst our opponents improve the shining hour by means peculiarly their own and energetically make good the position already gained, thereby realising the fondest desire of the Tory heart, viz.. Mr. Gladstone dethroned and kept at bay his whole life out?
"PROGRESS."

THE WARRINGTON HIGH RIP GANG. quite agree with " Reform's " letter in your last Issue, and consider the state of our streets certainly neces- sitates the immediate attention of the proper authorities. As a ratepayer, I am grateful to Mr. Councillor Dixon for bringing the matter before the Council at its hut sitting. Surely, enough has been said about the unruly throng that every Sunday evening parades our streets and carries on its "little game" to the disgust and annoyance of all respecta- ble pedestrians, without any apparent fear of the police; and also of the" High Rip Gang" type of humanity, thaticon- gregates night and day at the corners of our chief thorough- fares, spending time in the way only VA) accurately described by " Reform." There is anether class of people the police would do well to pay a little more attention to, I mean the vagrants, who do nothing but pester shopkeepers and private houses from Monday morning till Saturday nigl,t, and oftcn enough on the Sunday, asking for relief, but in nine cases out of ten wanting money to purchase drink. It is to be hoped trade-- men will not encourage such a set, the gteat majority of whom are nothing but gross imposters. When a few such specimens are taken in hand and tauiht a severe lesson, it may possibly have the effect of abating these growing nuisances.—Yours, &c.,
SHOPKEEPER.

Sir,—lt is well that attention has been called to the habit of roughs loitering about the corners of our principal thoroughfares, to the great annoyance of tradespeople. The grievance is a real one, kit your correspondent "Reform " hits rather too hard at the police, who cannot be at every corner at once. They seem to be constantly telling loiterers to "move on." which, I expect, is what tney are instructed to dc, but could not matters be taken in hand more firmly ? It is the opinion of your correspondent, and of many other townspeople, that if possible a number of these roughs who block up the narrow pavement should be either" run in," or summoned, and then dealt with in such a manner as would serve as a warning and a deterrent. While on this subject I should like to give a passing caution to any of your readers who are timid, or who object to foul language, to give Scotland-road a wide berth after nightfall. Many of the worst characters in town hang about there, with no very good intent, you may be sure, and I have heal d it stated at the Borough Police Court, I believe by the late Inspector Berry, that it was not safe for any respectable pirson to pass along that thoroughfare after dark. If it is so bad as to warrant a statement like that, surely strenuous means should be taken to retrieve its character. A regular study ef the police columns of the weekly papers reveals how many cases have been before the magistrates that have oc- curred, or had their origin, in Scotland-road, and I think one great reason of this state of affairs is not difficult to find. Any one knowing the locality will understat 3 what I mean.—yours, &c., Warrington, Nov. 4, 1886.

THE HOME RULE QUESTION. Sir,—For the informatidn of your readers I send you the following facts, taken from an official return compiled by order of 'the Riots Commission of Belfast, showing the man- ner in which this loyal town keeps up its reputation for religions intolerance, and also I submit obvious reasons why its " apostles " cry out so loudly against that measure of justice to Ireland—Home Rule. As long as .Orangemen are allowed to have all the plums of office all is well, but the moment any measure is proposed which will break down the barriers of religions intolerance and prejudice, and per- mit each one, no matter what his religious opinions, to take his fair 'there in the affairs of the country, then the cry is raised of the "Empire in danger," the Loyal minority will be crushed, Separation, ikc., and a score of other cries which were freely used during the late general election by Conser- vative and Unionist candidates. I see from your paper of Saturday last that Mr. A. Ben- nett opened the first meeting of the Holy 1 rinity Literary and Debating Society with a paper on "The Home of the Orangeman," and I am sorry that your report does not show whether Mr. Bennett mentioned to his audience the facts which I send yen, and of which he ought to have been aware—that is unless his paper was meant to suit his audi- ence. If, however, he did not, and he has since become acquainted with these facts, I would advise him to give them his close study, and rchallenge him or any opponent of Home Rule to point out a single town or city in Ireland where the population are so much more in proportion Catho- lic to Protestant, end where the same spirit of religious in- tolerance and bigotry is displayed. Now for the facte : There are seven officers in the Town Clerk's Office, inclu- ding himself, and not one of them is a Catholic. Total i paid n salaries, £2,775. in tbe occounts office there are five officers, not one being a Catholic. Total paid in salar- ie.!), £Bl5. In the cashier's office there are two, both Pro- testants. Total paid in salaries, £220. There are five rate collectors. Protestants, the commission for collection being li per cent. In the surveyor's office and department there are 22, four of thess being Roman Catholics. Total paid ii 4 salaries, £2,701, of which sum the four Catholics re- 't ve £2BO among them. The sanitary staff consists of kt officers, all Protestants except one, who disclaims ction with any denomination. Among them they trom the rates £964 103. annually. The officials iii Gas-works are all Protestants except the engineer tnaL,•er, who is a free lance, not being connected Aa i ny>denomination. They are six n all and lira an- -625 out of the rates. The Gas i as Offices employ 414,/all Protestants, and drawlD .n salaries .'"vitntially. Of the three market officials, one is a ''''ir total salaries ore £542, of which the Catho-

lie takes £ll7. The car inspectors are both Protestants, and take £l9O between them. There are four street inspec- tors, all Protestants, and taking annual in silaries £413. There are three functionaries, all Protestants, in connection with the cemetery and parks, and they draw annually in salaries £345. Dropping out the rate collectors, who are paid on commission, we find that the amount paid annually to its officials by the Belfast Corporation amounts to £14,040 10s., and that of this grand total the sum that falls to Roman Catholics is £397. Yours, dzc . FIAT JUSTITIA.

THE KNIGHTS OF LABOUR. Eir,—l do not know whether or not many of your readers have felt interested in the election of a Mayor for New York. They may have been too much taken up with the Bulgarian question and with the Conservative conference at Bradford last week, and the Liberal corference at Leeds this week, to spare a thought for what seems of so little importance as the election of a transatlantic Mayor; yet I venture to express the opinion that there is more significance in the result of that election than in fifty Bul- garian questiona, and, I was going to say fifty hundred party conferences, but I will merely say of any reasonable number of such pretentious, but essentially unimportant Con- claves. The significance of the New York election lies in the fact that, in a city which is the heart and centre of the great monopolies of the United States, the stronghold of the millionaires, and in face of electioneering tactics of the unscrupulousness of which people in this country have little conception, Mr. Henry George, the nominee of the great labour organisation, the Knights of Labour has been supported by nearly seventy thoesand votes. This is a great triumph of labour, and shows unmistakeably the kind of opinions that are gradually spreading amongst the masses of the United States, and it shows also that the Knights of Labour are acquiring a power that no other combination of labour has ever had. It may be some will think that Mr. George is a politician of much the same type as English workingmen members of Parliament, but this would be doing him a grievous injustice, for while these latter have given a lesson in ser- vility to party leaders that could have better been done without, Mr. George has en'irely repudiated any connection with either of the two great American parties. In the grossly prejudiced accounts of the election which have ap- peared in the English daily papers. Mr. George is des- cribed as a Socialist and sometimes even as an Anarchist, but, as anyone who is the least acquainted with his writings knows, he would be much more truthfully des- cribed as an anti-monopolist. His cardinal doctrine is that wherever monopolies, whether they be natural mono- polies such is land and minerals, or what are from the na- ture of things practical monopolies arch as railways, tramways, and the brewery business as carried on in Eng- land, are left in the hands of private individuals, the inevi- table result is that the monopolists get richer and the rest,' of the people poorer. From this he argues that as the value of monopolies is conferred by the people as a whole, it ought to be enj)yed by those who confer it. It is this doctrine that he has championed in New Yorg, and it is this doctrine that almost every third voter in New York has approved and supported. Surely this is a presage of changes in face of which such petty, reactionary, Tory red herrings as peasant proprietary, greater facilities for sale of glebe lands, transferring of payment of tithes from tenant to landlord and other things of that sort will be laugh l out of existence. It is to be hoped that the New York election will also have the effect of opening the eyes of English workmen to the value of the Knights of Labour organisation. It is not long since this order was formed, but in a few years it has proved by the rapidity of its growth, the power it has gained, and the work it has done, that it is the most effec- tive engine the working classes of any country have yet possessed for enforcing their claims. There are, I believe, a few branches in this country, and that they may grow and multiply is the wish of JAQUES.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

LONDON, THURSDAY. There are not many instances in political history of a public meeting wielding the far reaching in- fluence which was undoubtedly possessed by the gathering at Leeds yesterday. There is, of course, one other instance within recent memory, and to which Mr. John Morley referred with pardonable pride. This was the famous Leeds gathering, at which the policy of the Liberal party was embodied in the phrase" Franchise first." That was a memo- rable occason by reason of its influence upon the drift of political affairs. it is safe to predict that the meeting of yesterday will not fall short of it. Of course, the essential importance of the meeting lies in the fact that it was one of delegates. The biggest hall in Leeds was crowded to overflow, but ' nearly every man present represented a larger or smaller circle of staunch Liberals. It was really the National Liberal Party who were crowded in the hall, and who cheered the many principles set forth in simple but forcible language by Mr. Morley. Such a demonstration was sorely needed, and its accomplishment is most timely. The sneers and abuse daily launched at the head of Mr. Glad- , ' stone by a considerable section of the press cannot fail to have had a despondent effect. It is not for one newspaper to be answering another on this matter; but it is a very great thing when such a meeting as that of yesterday gathers, and with ringing cheers greets the name 02 the Old Leader. A gentleman who was present, and who has taken part in most of the great political gatherings of the last six years, tells me that he never saw anything equal to the effect created by Mr. Morley's indig- nantly spoken words—," We are not here to choose a leader; there is no vacancy." In a moment the vast audience was on its feet, the peals of cheering finally rounding off in the lilting music of a new popular song, which the excited organist, forgetful of decorum, incontinently accompanied. This must be personally gratifying to Mr. Gladstone, who, , with a mind so sensitive that it cannot overlook even Lord Brabourne, must feel acutely the stream of obloquy daily directed towards Hawarden. But of even larger account is the probable result upon the fortunes of the Liberal party and the welfare of the kingdom. Three things are now quite clear. First, that the Irish policy of Mr. Gladstone shall be sustained by the great bulk of the Liberal party; secondly, that any attempt on the part of the Government to postpone Irish business in the com- ing session shall be resisted ; and thirdly, that it is under the leadership of Mr. Gladstone that the Liberal party will now, as heretofore, go forward to victory. There were one or two little incidents at the great meeting at Leeds yesterday, which bring into strong light certain personal changes that have taken place within the last twelve months. First we may reckon the relative positions of Mr. John Morley and Sir William Harcourt. A year ago Mr. . John Morley, though then beginning to come to the front, would not have been reckoned as an equiva- lent to Sir II: illiam Harcourt as an attraction at a ' public meeting. Yesterday Mr. Morley took the ' first place, and almost totally eclipsed Sir William Harcourt. Another notable incident was that acci- dental mention of Mr. Bright's name at a monstre gathering of Liberals passed in silence, whilst a re- ference to Mr. Chamberlain was followed by a burst of hooting with difficulty repressed. Only one thing was unchanged, and that was the enthusiastic at- taehment of provincial Liberals to Mr. Gladstone. If there were any variation. in this feeling it was in the direction of accentuation. I dn't know how it may be in the country, where political insight is often keener than in London, but I can bear tes- timony that here, even among .Mr. Gladstone's friends, there is a feeling of surprise at the erqhu- siasm with which the old chiefs name was received yesterday. The new Lord Cairns, better known to fame as Lord Garmoyle, came into possession, amongst other goods, of a valuable law library. The late Lord Chancellorwas particularly proud of his rarely complete series of reports in the House of Lords, Privy Council, Chancery, Bankruptcy, and Common Law cases, the volumes of which would fill a moderately-sized room. He had also a complete set of 194 volumes of what is known to lawyers as the New Law Reports. Another of his treasures was a complete set, up to 1874, of Hansard, a work that mustered 323 volumes. Here was an opportunity for many days'. pleasant study by the new earl. But he does not seem to have cared for it, and yesterday

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURD tY, NOVEMBER 0, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURD tY, NOVEMBER 0, 1886.

this great library was dispersel under the auction- eer's hammer, going dirt cheap as compared with its original cost. Of the other latest additions to our hereditary legis- lators, the most noble the Marquis of Ailesbury, nothing has happily been heard. He appeared at his grandfather's funeral minus the big saucer buttons on his coat, which have hitherto been a cherished joy of his life. This was regarded as a sign of grace, an indication of intention to conform to more common-place aspects of life than have hitherto distinguised him. But those personally acquainted with his lordship are giving odds that the buttons will in due time flash upon the alarmed gaze of the Lord Chancellor seated upon the woolsack. Meanwhile public curiosity has been centred upon the relations between the new Marchioness and the dowager Marchioness, the famous Maria, Marchioness of Ailesbury. Her ladyship, known for brevity as "Lady A," is one of the best preserved and most indefatigable veterans of London society. During the season there is never a night on which the streets in which are situated the best houses do not resound with the cry for the carriage of" Maria, Marchioness of Ailesbury." Her ladyship can do more places in a single night than the freshest debutante. Every day from the middle of May to the middle of July the "Morning Post" has a little paragraph stating how Maria, Marchioness of Ailec- bury, dined last night with Lord So-and-so, or the Duke of Quelquechose. In the same newspaper, and in the society journals, the autumn days are gilded with the announcement of her ladyship's passage from country house to country house. What age she has reached no one dare venture to guess. Some say she is older than Lady Dorothy Neville, whilst her partisans deny it. Lady Dorothy will be known out of London society by her recent escapade in Kent, when the gushing young thing had herself photographed, her dress a tlaz3 of prim- roses, and a little figure of Mr. Gladstone peeping out of a jam pot. It was of this incident when recorded to him that Mr. Gladstone with unwonted cynicism observed, "Well, well, girls will be girls." Maria the Marchioness must, one would imagine, be a grim reality to Dolly the Marchioness. Dolly's real name was not Tester, as she was known at Brighton Theatre, and subsequently at the Caiety. Her parents were respectable working people named Halley, living at Brighton. Fourteen years ago she joined the ballet of the Brighton Theatre, taking her mother's maiden name of Tester. From Bria,hton she went to live under the sacred lamp of burlesque which . Mr. Hollingshead kept brightly burning, and it was there that Lord Severnake saw her. She is six years older than the Marquis, and by so much closer in sympathy with "Lady A." The dissatisfaction of the position of the pro- posed Imperial Institute, as far as it has been authoritatively indicated, is daily growing. The proceedings hitherto have certainly not been pro- mising. It is a noteworthy fact that not one of the leading newspapers has backed up the proposal of the Prince of Wales, whilst one or two hav3 pointed out its impracticability. What underlies the whole affair is the suspicion that the Prince of Wales is being made use of for the personal advan- tage of a certain clique who have been prominent in connection with the great exhibitions at South Kensington. Two things are already pretty broad- ly determined upon. One .is that the site of the proposed institute shall not be fixed at South Ken- sington, and the other is that there shall not be any- thing of Cremorne about the Institute. This latter objection receives the powerful support of the idely extended circle connected with theatres and other places of amusement. This includes not only the proprietors, but the actors and their friends, literary men, journalists, and newspaper conductors, who are bound to protect the interests represented by steady advertising custom. There is no doubt that theatres and music halls have grievously suf- fered by the existence of the Colinderies nd its predecessors, and all connected with them look with consternation upon the prospect of permanently es- tablishing such a formidable rival. In this they have the public support. Obviously an Imperial Institute founded by national subscriptions should be something more serious than a modern Cre- morne. Mr. Whistler, familiarly known as "Our James," is packing up for his visit to America. He is taking with him all his best kno pictures and por.aaits, which he intends to exhibit in New York and Boston. Mr. Whistler proposes to remain in the United States for about three months. But it is probable his picl urea may return to London before the end of that time. The Society of Biitish Artists, of which he is the president, intend to pay him the compliment of getting up an exhibiticn composed entirely of his pictures, after the fashion of the recent Millais' exhibition. Mr. Whistler is under the direction of Mr. D'Oyley Carte, who has made arrangements for his delivering in the princi- pal cities of the United States his quaint " Ten o'clock." This is recommended to the _nerican taste by the circumstance that it has been delivered only once in England. "I refused .to repeat it in London," Mr. Whistler loftily says, in a letter he wrote last month to a friend in the States. There are, or course, two ways of looking at this fact. Mr. Whistler, with all his eccentricity, is an ex- ceedingly shrewd man, and if the "Ten o'clock" had been as successful as was hoped from the in- genious manner in which it was advertised there would, I fancy, have been no diffirmlty in repeating it. Mr. D'Oyley Carte thinks it will do for the United States, and he is a judge.

FIR g AT R MSGATE. FOUR PER6ONS BURNED TO DEATH.

A very serious fire occurred at Rarnsgate at half-past four on Friday morning, which resulted in four persons being burned to death, these being an aid lady named Warden, her two grandcbildien, and their aunt. The house where the fire broke out is a four-storeyed buildieg, situate in Cliff-street, near the Old Marine Library. Two men wbo passed it at half-past four o'clock did not notice anything atni. I, but at a quarter to five the whole house was abkza. The occupier, a young stonemason named ‘Vardea, got on to the roof of the next house and exclairneel, " For God's sake, save my wife and children !" Those who had reached the spot produced. a ladder from some raw truildings, and proceeded to attempt a rescue, led he Police-constable Williams. The wife, with the in- fant in her arms, climbed to the top of the bow viralow, and then fell fainting. The child was taken down safely be a voun; man named Davi:on, and the constable, with two other men, succeeded in getting the woman down. She was very much burnt a out the lower part of the body and limbs, and she had to be taken to the intirtnaty in a very precarious state. Williams then endeavoured to do further service, but was overcome by the awoke, sod swooned in descending the ladder. He quickly came to, however, and wanted to make another attempt, but was held back, any further effort to save life being obviously impossible of success. The fire brigade quickly arrived, and managed to confine the fire to the premi. es, but only after the four remaining inmates had been burned to death. The body of Mrs. Warden was found in the ruins about eight o'clock frighully charred, and the fire brigade and police subse- quently recovered the remains of the aunt, Miss Betts, who, with one of the little Wardens in her arms, was dit?overed in a corner of a top room which had not falls.' in. Another child's body remains to be discovered. The origin of the fire has not yet been ascertained.

NEW YORIE, FRlDAY.—Accordina to intelligence received here the Mexican papers report that General Ci-areia de la Cadena has been shut for high treason.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT. 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The active demand for money, which was a feature of the early part of the week,bas subsided on the release of the huge amount of application money sent in to duinness and Ca. Business on the Stock Exchange has continued quiet, but prices have been firm, home railsparticularly remaining healthy. More than once lately I have warned my readers against the contagion of the gold fever now raging. My pessimism has been amply and remarkably justified this week by the Premier of Queensland. wbo has officially raised his voice against the mania, and denounced the majority of these mines as snares and delusions. Almost immediately following on this utterance comes the reports from the Kimberly mines, which are described by unbias.Led reporters as a " huge failure." The retural result of this has been a complete reaction, Which has aiready begun to manifest itself in a big fall in the mining market. The Guinness boom has not paesed off without incident. Great dissatisfaction is expressed at the partial manner in which the allotment has been made. The shares having gone to a large premium, it is naturally to the interest of ttscs3" in the swim" to hold them. The city editors have all remarked the signiic-ant influ- ence exerted by a prominent outside broker upon the last settlement on the Stock Exchange by the maknitude of his operations. The extraordinary growth of the system of outside deal- ing has proved a heavy blow to the mystery and redtapeisin that has hitherto enshrouded the Stock Exchange, and the public have been educated by this means to a remarkable degree in matters appertaining to the money market. Since the system was first introduced by the Abbotts till its present extensive development by such as the Broad-street firm of J. Lewis Mias di Co., Limited, who introduced the half per cent, cover system, the public have had facilities for speculation never dreamed of before, and the effect has been to draw weekly from the provincesthousands of pounds that would otherwise haye been idle. The well-known London house of Hermann Loog have issued a prospectus inviting subscriptions for a capital of £150,000 in Li shares.. The success of this rerr irkable. firm has been largely owing to its possession of various ' valuable patents which have been worked with extraordin- ary enterprise. The house has over 50 branches and sub- depots in the Kingdom, se well as a second head centre in Glasgow. A very noticeable feature of this undertaking is that the vendor takes no cash, all the money subscribed I going into the business.

FELEEMASONRY.—The annual installation meeting of the members of the Cholmondeley Lodge. 1,908, took plate en Wednesday, at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsham. After the transaction of some introductory business, the auditors pre- sented the balance sheet for the year, and spoke in most eulogistic terms of the iLdefatigable services rendered by the treasurer, through whose emertions, mainly, the funds of the lodge were in such a flourishing condition. The rtport was unanimously adopted. Bro. Salmon then installed Bro. Ashton into the chair of Worshipful Master in a very im- pressive manner. The following officers were subsequently invested :—Bro. H. E. Heywood, I.P.M. ; Bro. T. H. Hit- chen, S.W. ; Bro. C. H. Lewini J. W.; Bro. G. Hammond Danby, treasurer (re-appointed) ; Bro. James Reynolds, secretary ; Bro. James Salmon, D. of C. ; Bro. H. Harrisson, S.D. ; Bro. J. Walwyn-White, J.D.; Bro. T. Wooliscroft, I.G. ; Bro. John Humphreys, organi.t ; and Bro. John Roberts, re-elected tyler. At the-conclusion of the business the brethren dined together, under the presidency of the W.M., the catering of Miss Baker, of Chester, being of the best class. The usual loyal and Masonic toasts were pro- posed during the evening. The musical arrangements were carried out by the organist, assisted by Bros. Webster., Williams, W. R. Knowles, Hughes, Walwyn-White, and Griffiths.

LATEST NEWS.
The Right Hen. John Bright, M.P., has arrived at Llan- dudno for his anncal autumn holidays, and will remain some time.

Mr. J. H. de Ricci, who unsuccessfully contested Bedford, is now mentioned as the probable Conservative candidate for Brighton. John Nott, a porter at Newport Pagnell Railway Station, was killed by a passing train on Thursday night as he was crossiag the line.

The" Morning Post" understands that his Royal High- ness the Duke of Connaught has been appointed to the com- mand of the Bombay Arms'. In a billiard match at Westminister Aquarium. on Thur..- day night, Peali made an unfinished break of 2,002 with 333 and 361 consecutive spot strokes. The Duke of Portland will grant 150 allotment gardens at Fluncknall next spring. Eighty gardens have already been allotted. There is a great demand for them among the workmen.

CABINET MEETING.—A Cabinet Council, originally fixed for Saturday, to,4k place on Friday afternoon at half-past two, Lord Salisbury came to town specially to meet his colleagues, all of whom were present. The chief question under consideration was the present state of affairs in Ire- land.

THE LONDON SOCIALISTS.—The Central News is enabled to confirm the announcement that some working-men's organisations have resolved to resent the interference of the Socialists by breaking up their meeting or demonstration in Trafalgar-square on Lord Mayor's day. The authorities have, however, prohibited the proposed meeting as well as the proposed procession. PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO MR. GLADSTONE.—RepIy- Iag to a letter from a leading Liberal in Warwick, who had suggested the presentation to him of a national testimonial in recognition of his long public services, Mr. Glaistone writes :—" I do not desire and I should regret the presen- tation to me of any national testimonial, eval if it sprang from a feeling wildly spread, which I do not think exists.

THE IMPRISONED MANCHESTER MINISTER.—A reply has been received with regard to the case of the Rev. James Mackie, pastor of the Scotch Church in Manchaster, recently sentenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labour for assaulting an elder of the church in the vestry. The Home Secretary intimates that he is unable to discover grounds to justify him in advising any interference with the sentence.

ATTEMPT TO UPSET THE SCOTCH EspuEss.—Tho young man named Thomas Jones and William Burden (one em- ployed by the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany) were arrested at Crewe on Friday on the charge of Placing an obstruction upon the railway. On Wednesday vight the Scotch mail for Euston oacountered several large iron bolts across both rails near Liverpool bridge,and it wrs almost a miracle that the train kept on the rails.

div.head: IMPORTANT TRADE MARK PROSECUTION.
div.p: IMPORTANT TRADE MARK PROSECUTION.

A case of some importance- to, mineral water manufacturers, the first of the kind that has come. before the Warrington' magistrates, was heard at Warrington Borough Court yesterday. Robert Maskell, shopkeeper, Church-street, was summoned for having, on the 22nd Obtober; sold bottles of ginger beer,bearing the trademarks,cf Eddowes and Co., and Hugh Fairhurst and Co., boji of Warring- to_i. The proceedings were instituted by the Man- cl.este and District MineraliWaterTinde Protection Society, for whom • Mr. Jenkins appeared. The association is one formed-toprotect the interests of its members, and Mr. Jenkins explained the Act under which the case was brought, and which made it illegal for anyone to use bottles bearing the trad- mark of a firm that did not sell its bottles. Mr; John Greave, an inspector of the association, appeared as prosecutor. Mr. Jenkins having put in evidence proof of registration, said that Mr. Cireave on the day in question went to the shop oftlie defendant, and purchased seven bottles of ginger beer, four of which bore the name and trade 'mark of. Hugh Fair- hurst and Co. There had been: a decision given by Mr. Raffles, Liverpool stipendiary, inwhich he said lie was not quite satisfied that there was any inten- tion to do what was wrong or- defraud' the owners of the bottles, but in this case it would be proved that defendant had been cautioned, and was aware of the risk she ran. Evidence -as to the purchase of the bottles having been given by Mr. Greave, Mr. Arthur Edclowes said that about three years ago he saw some of the bottles of the firm to which h be- longed at the defendant's shop, and cautioned her against using them. The three bottles,produced bore the trade mark of the firma Mr. Greenough, of the firm of Fairhurst and CO., said that the firm lost between £2OO and ,f.,'3CO a year through the•improper use of bottles. Evidence • was • also given by Mr. William Eddowes. Defendant, whose wife ap- peared, was fined .E 1 and costs, ..E2 18A ed in all. She cried, and declared that her husband was ill, and she was not in a position to pay the Jae.

div.head: ALLEGED:ELOP EIIF,NT AND ROBBERY
div.p: ALLEGED:ELOP EIIF,NT AND ROBBERY
AT WARRINGTON.

A heartless case of elopement is reported to have taken place from Warrington this weel6 It ap- pears that Thomas Goodier, a shoemaker, who lives at Green's-row, Latchford, has for some considerable time had lodging with him an old lady named Woodcock, who is 71 years of age. Mrs. Woodcock has a son named James, a married man, who has been in America. Recently he returned home to England and went to lodge with his ,mother at Latchford. His wire, it is said, was living. at Man- chester. Woodcock discovered that his mother had a sum of £l4O invested in Parrs Bank,and he suc- ceeded in persuading her to allow him to withdraw themoney, so that it could be re-invested in his own name. It is said that he took advantage- of this permission and drew the money, afterwards invest- ing £3O in the Post Office Savings Bank for the use of his mother. Woodcock and the wife of Goodier I seem to have become too intimate, for early this I week Goodier found to hi dismay that the faith- less wife and the new lodger were missing. It is supposed that she went with Woodcock, taking with her two of the chilthen of her marriage, both boys, one aged 3 and the other 6 years. Afterwards the deserted husband received a telegram, which was fDllowed by a letter, from his wife, informing I him that she was on her way to America. At the Borough Pollee Court, yesterday morn- ing, the deserted husband and the deserted wife I appeared before the magistrates and stated how they were situated, their idea evi- dently being to obtain, a warrant, or warrants, to bring back the runaways. It was alleged that Woodcock had taken away property not his own. iChief Constable Hunt asked what good a warrant would be, as the couple would now be almost at America, and they could not be fetched home? Mrs Woodcock statel that she was left in a dest'- tute condition, and the Chief Constable remarked that.she had better make an application to the Board of Guardians at Manchester, where she was living. Mrs Woodcock expressed the belief that her husband had not gone to America, but was in ; London, and the disconsolate pair, on being told that the magistrates. could not assiSt atzem, left I the court.

GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.—On .Tuesday the monthly meeting of: this Board was held in the schools, Great Sankey. There were present Mersrs. Turner (chairman)., Kerfoot, Hougoton, Ridgway, Cook, and S. Sutton (clerk). The Clerk reported that the total income during the past. year, includ- ing loans, had been £3,258 3s 4d, and the total ex- penditure, including the expenditure from the loan: had been £2,850 13s 9d, leaving a balance in hand after certain deductions of £4Ol Os rd. The Chair- man inquired if they had got all the bills in on their capital charges. The Clerk said that he had not, as he was waiting for the contractoreand archit cts' bills. The Clerk -also brought forward an estimate of expenditure for the coming year, from which it appeared that in addition to the, school fe-,, and balance in hand of about £ll3, £240., as against £230 last year, would? be rer,uired from the overseers, which would mean a rate of 4d in-the X for the half year. He explained that he was not taking into account in this estimate the grant to be received from the Education Department, because owing to a change in the time of examination tbat grant would not be received before the-financial year had expired. When they did receive the grant it would be for seventeen months instead of twelve, so he expected that in the followincryear the rate would go down to 3d or 4d in the £7 The Chairman said if they brought the rate down, to that extent they would have done what no other School Board in the kingdom had done. Mr. Keribot thought the ac- counts very satisfactory, though they would not look so well for the ratepayers this year. The Clerk said they were not going beyond the amount they specified, 4d in the X for the half year. The Chair- man said they always laid themselves out to keep the rate from getting beyond 8d in the £ when t)king into account the grant, and they were not going to exceed that without the grant. The ac- counts and estimate were-adopted, and it was agreed to call upon the overseers for the sum of 1120 to meet expenses up to March next. The Chairman called the attention of' the Board to the manner in which the ground in front of the school had been laid out and planted % and said they were indebted to Mr. Kerfoot for the trouble he had taken in regard to this matter. The rest of the members agrhed with the chairman's remarks, and considered the front of the school had been much improved. This was all the business of public interirs' t.. Mr. C. R. M. Talbot, M.P.," father" of the House of the Commons, has announced an abatetwat at 24 per cent to the tenants on his estates in Wales,

"-EARLY METFODIST AZ" BEINSEY ROAD GHAPEL.—On Thursday evening, a service of praise, illustrative of the singing and order of wor- ship of the early Methodist Church, was held in Bewsey-road Chapel, in connection with the Silver- street Sunday School Band- of Rope. The musical part of the service consisted of many of the choicest Methodist hymns; set to the oldest of old times; and the singing et the large congre- :gation, led by an efficient instrumental band, the members of which had kindly given their services, and the united choirs' of Sankey-Bridge and Bewsey Road Chapels, together with a number of the Band of Hope children, the, whole under the able con- ductorship of Mn. TERRIBLE EXPLOSION AT HULL
EIGHT MEN KILLED.

On Thursday afternoon a terrible explosion oc-- curred on board the Newcastle steamer Cartago Nova, which had arrived at Hull from Alexandria on the previous day. The vessel was discharging her cargo itf the Albert Dock at Hull when her donkey boiler exploded, instantly killing fcur men, one of whom was blown to the top of a very high warehouse. Two men died on reaching the Royal Infirmary. Belween 20 and 30 men were injured, some of them at> seriously that they are not ex- pected to recover: During the time of discharging several men from an engine shop were on b)ard . doing repairs to the main bailers and engines, and there was thus a large numbev of men an board the steamer. The violence of the explosion was shown. by the great distance to wLich portions of the boiler were blown.
Of the fifteen injund taken to the Royal Infir- mary, through the boii;n- egplosi,)n, two more have since died, making tho total frilmber of deaths eight..
